Frequency Lock Encoding

Joshua Montierth

Degree
Master of Science, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Brigham Young University

April 2027 (expected)

Keywords

Download PDF · 95 pages

Abstract

Wireless communication links carry an inherent inefficiency—they possess more synchronization capacity than is required under most operating conditions. This thesis presents and evaluates Frequency Lock Encoding (FLE), a physical-layer wireless subprotocol that exploits this underutilized communication capacity. FLE enables a secondary parallel stream of data on top of existing wireless protocols through controlled frequency offsets that are interpreted as noise by an unaware receiver. The mathematical framework underlying this technique is analyzed for both single- and multi-carrier protocols. The subprotocol is then evaluated through simulation across a wide range of operational parameters and transmission channel conditions. FLE is subsequently implemented on software-defined radios (SDRs) and later adapted to commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware. Finally, applications in steganography, spectrum coordination, and wireless network security are presented, showing some of the many potential applications for utilizing this latent signaling space.

Keywords: Subprotocol, Physical Layer, Spectrum Coordination, Wireless Network Security, Steganography

1 Introduction

Wireless links face unpredictable impairments—thermal noise, device motion, temperature drift, interference, oscillator irregularities, and even subtle shifts along a wavefront—that introduce errors into transmitted signals. To ensure reliability under extreme operating conditions, protocols are designed with powerful synchronization mechanisms that reserve additional bandwidth and correction capability to handle impairments that may only rarely occur. Most of the time, however, systems operate well within their correction envelope, and this excess synchronization capacity sits unused.

Traditionally, analog impairments have been viewed solely as problems to eliminate. Modulation schemes are carefully tuned to balance throughput and reliability, and because synchronization failure is catastrophic, designers consistently “overshoot,” provisioning systems for worst-case conditions. The result is a latent surplus of synchronization and correction power that, under ordinary conditions, is treated as dead weight.

This thesis proposes a paradigm shift in how impairments and synchronization overhead are viewed in wireless communication. Instead of allowing this surplus correction capacity to remain idle, we intentionally introduce controlled, meaningful perturbations into the signal that occupy the same space currently reserved for natural noise. These perturbations are not random disturbances, but carefully engineered modifications that remain entirely within the correction bounds of the synchronization loops. As a result, a legacy receiver absorbs them while still recovering the original message with little to no degradation. To a receiver that knows how to interpret them, however, the perturbations encode a second, parallel stream of information. In this way, what was once wasted synchronization margin becomes a new signaling resource: a secondary communication layer operating simultaneously with the primary protocol without requiring additional spectrum, extra antennas, or changes to the underlying communication standard. This is akin to adding additional lanes to an already existing spectrum highway, enabling more traffic to coexist within the same physical medium.

A subprotocol is a communication protocol that operates on top of an already existing one without impacting the performance of the primary protocol. Prior work has explored a variety of approaches to implement subprotocols, including inter-packet delays [1], RF noise [2], special Wi-Fi frames [3], or channel state information [4]. This thesis presents Frequency Lock Encoding (FLE), a fully developed wireless subprotocol that embeds information through controlled frequency perturbations applied directly to the underlying communication waveform. Because FLE operates through the same synchronization mechanisms already present in wireless receivers, it is inherently protocol-agnostic—meaning it can operate on top of virtually any wireless protocol regardless of its framing structure, modulation format, or higher-layer implementation. Since every known wireless protocol requires some form of carrier frequency synchronization, there exists a mechanism through which FLE can operate.

FLE is also inherently backward-compatible. A receiver unaware of the subprotocol simply interprets the intentional perturbations as ordinary noise and continues normal operation without modification. A properly functioning subprotocol therefore leaves the primary communication effectively intact while enabling secondary communication in parallel. This compatibility allows FLE to integrate into existing wireless infrastructure without requiring changes to deployed hardware or protocol standards.

The proposed approach is also fundamentally opportunistic. The subprotocol consumes only the excess impairment-correction capacity available in the primary communication link. Under operating conditions where the full synchronization capability of the receiver is needed for the primary communication, the secondary signaling can be reduced or disabled entirely without altering the operation of the primary system.

While there are many possible ways to introduce meaningful perturbations into a communication system, this work focuses specifically on controlled frequency offsets. The choice of frequency-domain perturbations over other synchronization domains, such as timing, is intentional. Frequency synchronization loops generally do not suffer from self-noise in the same manner as timing recovery loops, resulting in a cleaner observable signal. Furthermore, although carrier synchronization is commonly implemented in hardware, the outputs of these algorithms are frequently exposed to firmware or software layers, unlike many synchronization mechanisms in other domains. This accessibility enables practical implementation on both software-defined radios (SDRs) and commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) wireless hardware.

There are many potential applications of such a technology, with additional opportunities left for future work. The primary contributions of this thesis are summarized as follows:

  • Introduction and development of Frequency Lock Encoding (FLE) as a protocol-agnostic, backward-compatible, opportunistic wireless subprotocol.

  • Mathematical analysis of FLE operation on both single-carrier and multi-carrier modulation schemes.

  • Simulation and evaluation of FLE performance across a variety of wireless channel models.

  • Implementation and validation of FLE using software-defined radios (SDRs).

  • Adaptation of FLE for commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware through manipulation of microprocessor firmware.

  • Presentation of novel applications of FLE technology in wireless steganography and spectrum coordination (UnderTone) as well as physical-layer wireless security (SpectralSeal).

1.1 System Overview

The core mechanism of FLE is illustrated in Figure 1.1. The transmitter introduces small, controlled frequency offsets into its carrier signal. These offsets encode secondary data as a frequency-shift keyed (FSK) modulation applied on top of the primary waveform. Each transmitted frame carries a deliberate carrier-frequency perturbation whose magnitude and sign map to a subprotocol symbol. On the receive side, every modern wireless receiver already estimates the carrier-frequency offset (CFO) between itself and the incoming transmitter as part of its normal synchronization process. A standard receiver treats these perturbations as ordinary oscillator drift and corrects them transparently, recovering the primary data with little to no degradation. An FLE-aware receiver, however, reads the per-frame CFO estimates and demodulates them to recover the secondary data stream.

The key insight is that the perturbations occupy the same parameter space as natural impairments—crystal drift, temperature variation, Doppler shift—and remain within the correction capability of the receiver’s synchronization loops. The subprotocol therefore coexists with the primary communication without additional spectrum, extra antennas, or modifications to the underlying standard.

This work investigates FLE under two implementation schemes: a complete-access scenario using software-defined radios (SDRs), where the transmitter and receiver have full control over the IQ samples; and a constrained-access scenario using commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) Wi-Fi hardware, where the radio is managed by closed-source firmware. In the latter case, we demonstrate that strategic reading and writing of undocumented hardware registers enables a fully functional FLE system despite the lack of direct baseband access.

This last point deserves emphasis, because it determines what deploying FLE would actually cost. Both halves of the mechanism are already present in commodity silicon. On the receive side, every wireless receiver estimates carrier frequency offset as part of normal synchronization, so the subprotocol observable is computed whether or not anyone reads it. On the transmit side, the carrier is synthesized by a tunable element—a fractional-NN divider in the hardware used here—so imposing the overlay is a matter of retuning at the subprotocol symbol rate rather than of adding signal-processing hardware. Neither end requires new silicon. What they require is access: the relevant registers must be exposed through the software stack, which on the platforms studied in this thesis meant discovering them experimentally, and which a vendor could instead provide in firmware. Where that access is granted, FLE is a software feature of hardware that already exists, and both the transmitter and the receiver of Chapter 4 are built this way on unmodified devices.

1.2 Related Work

FLE sits at the intersection of several active research areas in wireless communications. This section surveys the state of the art in spectrum sharing, wireless steganography, and physical-layer security, and identifies where FLE contributes to each.

1.2.1 Spectrum Coordination and Sharing

The dominant approach to large-scale spectrum coordination is centralized database management. The Citizens Broadband Radio Service (CBRS) relies on a Spectrum Access System (SAS) [5], and Wi-Fi 6E uses Automated Frequency Coordination (AFC) providers [6] to assign channels based on device locations and propagation models. While effective at the macro level, these systems require GPS capabilities and consistent internet backhaul—single points of failure that render them poorly suited for edge devices or disconnected environments. Furthermore, polling a centralized database is inherently too coarse-grained in time, space, and frequency for rapid, localized sharing decisions.

To address these limitations, various ad hoc spectrum-sharing protocols have been proposed that modify transmission characteristics to embed coordination data directly in the waveform. Existing approaches include embedding data into an OFDM subcarrier [7] and altering signal amplitude [8]. Some subprotocols have been developed for spectrum coordination as well by utilizing on-off keying across a sequence of transmissions [9] and manipulating inter-transmission timing [1], [10]. These methods share the goal of decentralized coordination, but are typically limited to tens of bits per second and tightly coupled to a single protocol.

FLE offers a distinct approach by encoding coordination data in the carrier-frequency offsets of an existing transmission. This yields substantially higher data rates—hundreds of kbps on SDRs—while operating in parallel with the primary data stream. Critically, a receiving device need not demodulate the primary payload to extract the secondary information; it must only estimate the carrier-frequency offset, a computation that every wireless receiver already performs. In practice, the most harmful spectrum collisions occur between devices using the same or closely related waveforms on independent, uncoordinated networks. Such devices already implement comparable carrier synchronization loops, making them inherently capable of observing FLE perturbations even without network association. FLE therefore provides a lightweight mechanism for implicit cross-network signaling—sharing frequency plans, channel usage, or other spectral metadata—without requiring primary network interoperability or higher-layer cooperation.

1.2.2 Wireless Steganography

Steganography—hiding data in plain sight—has a long history in digital media and has more recently been explored in the wireless domain. The concept of leveraging waveform parameters to embed secondary data has been studied extensively [11]–[14]. Approaches range from manipulating constellation points to emulate noisy channel conditions [11] to synthesizing hardware-like noise signatures via machine learning [12]. Classen et al. [14] conducted the work most closely aligned with FLE, exploring multiple covert channels for Wi-Fi systems, including the use of carrier frequency offsets.

Their scheme applies a static carrier frequency offset to each Wi-Fi frame and recovers it from the preamble’s frequency estimate. The offsets span 1–50 kHz and are selected empirically per platform: below roughly 5 kHz the covert channel becomes unreliable, and above roughly 10 kHz the legitimate frame error rate begins to rise. Because the offset is held constant over a frame and read from a per-frame estimator, the achievable rate is tied to the frame rate rather than to the symbol rate, yielding 250 kbps for 802.11a/g. Their implementation is also strictly limited to SDRs, never reached consumer hardware, and applies only to Wi-Fi.

FLE improves on these ideas in several ways. First, it can utilize much smaller offsets, allowing for finer granularity and consequently higher data rates.a FLE also generalizes many of the principles used in previous work, allowing frequency perturbations to be applied to arbitrary wireless protocols. We develop the theory for FLE for both single- and multi-carrier protocols, as well as for protocols that use continuous streams or framing. Rather than treating the offset as a fixed perturbation, FLE treats it as a general modulating waveform, allowing the subprotocol to be shaped by an arbitrary pulse shape.

a Our Wi-Fi implementation of FLE can successfully differentiate symbols with offsets on the order of hundreds of Hz rather than thousands.

Additionally, rather than tuning the offset empirically on a specific platform, Chapter 2 derives the admissible range of frequency deviation and subprotocol symbol rate in closed form from the base protocol’s loop bandwidth and damping, so the operating point transfers to any receiver whose carrier synchronizer is characterized and known. Finally, FLE is developed as a fully functioning subprotocol with framing, error correction, and rate adaptation—features typically absent from covert channel demonstrations that focus on evading detection rather than reliable data delivery—and, as Chapter 4 shows, it runs on unmodified commodity hardware rather than only on SDRs.

FLE exhibits strong steganographic properties: the perturbations occupy the same parameter space as natural oscillator impairments and are transparently absorbed by any standard receiver. A formal analysis of detectability—whether the per-frame CFO sequence under FLE is statistically distinguishable from natural drift—is an important direction for future work, but is beyond the scope of this thesis.

1.2.3 Physical-Layer Wireless Security

Rogue access points (RAPs) represent a persistent vulnerability in wireless network security. By establishing unauthorized infrastructure that mimics legitimate networks, attackers can intercept traffic, harvest credentials, and execute man-in-the-middle attacks [15]. Despite decades of research, the problem remains unsolved because each layer of defense introduces its own weaknesses [16].

At the protocol level, WPA3 introduced the Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) handshake and mandatory Protected Management Frames (PMF) [17] to prevent eavesdropping and deauthentication attacks that RAPs often employ. However, WPA3’s transition mode—which allows WPA2 and WPA3 clients to coexist on the same network—reintroduces downgrade vulnerabilities that an attacker can exploit to force legacy handshakes [18], [19]. WPA Enterprise with 802.1X certificate-based authentication provides stronger guarantees, but its deployment complexity limits adoption to managed corporate environments; the vast majority of consumer and small-business networks rely on pre-shared keys, where a rogue AP with the correct passphrase is indistinguishable from the legitimate one at the protocol level.

Traditional RAP detection systems operate above the physical layer, relying on MAC address filtering, behavioral traffic analysis, and RSSI fingerprinting [20]. These metrics are straightforward for a sophisticated attacker to spoof: MAC addresses can be cloned, traffic patterns imitated, RSSI values approximated by adjusting transmit power.

Physical-layer authentication offers a fundamentally harder-to-forge alternative. RF fingerprinting techniques exploit manufacturing variations in oscillators, power amplifiers, and other analog components to identify individual devices from their transmitted waveforms [21], [22]. While promising, these methods are passive—they characterize whatever hardware imperfections happen to exist—and their accuracy degrades with changing environmental conditions, receiver hardware, and device aging.

FLE enables an active physical-layer authentication approach: legitimate access points embed a cryptographic signature or device identifier directly into the carrier-frequency dynamics of every transmitted frame. Because the watermark resides in the physical layer rather than the payload, it survives higher-layer header stripping and is invisible to standard receivers. A monitoring device equipped with the appropriate verification parameters can authenticate frames in real time, while frames from rogue devices—which lack the correct FLE modulation—are immediately identifiable. Unlike passive RF fingerprinting, this approach does not depend on stable hardware imperfections; the authentication signal is deterministic and verifiable.

2 Mathematical Analysis

Frequency Lock Encoding comprises two wireless communication systems: the base protocol and the subprotocol. The following analysis will first treat a generic single-carrier modulation, representative of any underlying linear protocol. It will then be extended to the multi-carrier case, exploring the similarities and differences in implementation. The purpose of this analysis is to explore, quantitatively, the design parameters of the FLE system and their impact on the underlying protocol, finding the region where both primary and subprotocol can coexist without impacting each other’s performance.

2.1 Single-Carrier Analysis

In FLE for single-carrier modulation, the base protocol is a linear modulation whose complex-valued lowpass equivalent waveform [23] is

s(t)=∑k=−∞∞akp(t−kTs)s(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}a_{k}\,p(t-kT_{s})(2.1)

where

  • ak=a_{k}= the kk-th symbol drawn from the alphabet AA comprising MM (generally complex-valued) elements (e.g., the 16-QAM alphabet);

  • p(t)=p(t)= a unit-energy pulse shape defined on the interval T1≤t≤T2T_{1}\le t\le T_{2} (e.g., the square-root raised cosine pulse shape);

  • Ts=T_{s}= the symbol time (s/symbol) for the base protocol; the reciprocal is the symbol rate for the base protocol.

The symbols are assumed to be an iid sequence of equally-likely random variables with average symbol energy EavgE_{avg}.

In normal circumstances, the real-valued bandpass signal is created from (2.1) using [23]

sbp(t)=Re{s(t)ej2πf0t}s_{bp}(t)=\mathrm{Re}\{s(t)e^{j2\pi f_{0}t}\}(2.2)

The up-conversion of ss to sbps_{bp} is assumed to be performed by an I/Q mixer.

When the FLE subprotocol is used, the up-conversion step is modified, either in software or hardware. The real-valued bandpass signal is instead created from (2.1) using

sbp(t)=Re{s(t)ej(2πf0t+ϕ(t))}s_{bp}(t)=\mathrm{Re}\{s(t)e^{j(2\pi f_{0}t+\phi(t))}\}(2.3)

where the time-varying phase is due to the subprotocol and is described next.

The subprotocol consists of the PAM waveform given by

s~(t)=∑k~=−∞∞a~k~p~(t−k~T~s)\tilde{s}(t)=\sum_{\tilde{k}=-\infty}^{\infty}\tilde{a}_{\tilde{k}}\tilde{p}(t-\tilde{k}\tilde{T}_{s})(2.4)

where

  • a~k~=\tilde{a}_{\tilde{k}}= the k~\tilde{k}-th symbol drawn from the alphabet 𝒜~\tilde{\mathcal{A}} comprising M~\tilde{M} real elements (e.g., the binary alphabet);

  • p~(t)=\tilde{p}(t)= a pulse shape defined on the interval T~1≤t≤T~2\tilde{T}_{1}\le t\le\tilde{T}_{2} and normalized to unity DC gain, P~(0)=1\tilde{P}(0)=1, so that a constant symbol +A~+\tilde{A} produces a constant frequency deviation of exactly fdA~f_{d}\tilde{A} Hz;a

    a This normalization, rather than unit energy, is the one for which fdf_{d} is a frequency in hertz and the design parameter fdTsf_{d}T_{s} is dimensionless. It is also what a practical pulse-shaping filter implements: the square-root raised-cosine taps used in Chapter 3 are generated with a DC gain of one sample per symbol, so a steady subprotocol symbol shifts the carrier by fdA~f_{d}\tilde{A} and nothing else. The pulse train (2.4) is applied to a frequency modulator with frequency deviation fdf_{d} to produce the complex-valued lowpass equivalent signal [24]

ejϕ(t)e^{j\phi(t)}(2.5)

where the instantaneous phase is

ϕ(t)=2πfd∫0ts~(u)du\phi(t) = 2\pi f_{d}\int_{0}^{t}\tilde{s}(u)du(2.6)
ϕ(t)=2πfd∑k~=−∞∞a~k~∫0tp~(u−k~T~s)du\phantom{\phi(t)} = 2\pi f_{d}\sum_{\tilde{k}=-\infty}^{\infty}\tilde{a}_{\tilde{k}}\int_{0}^{t}\tilde{p}(u-\tilde{k}\tilde{T}_{s})du(2.7)

The FLE subprotocol for single carrier modulation is summarized by the system in Figure 2.1. The FLE subprotocol will not significantly degrade the performance of the base protocol if the base protocol phase estimator is able to track out the phase variations induced by the subprotocol. A decision-directed phase-locked loop is the assumed phase synchronizer for the base protocol, though a data-aided model would behave similarly. The factors that determine tracking capability of the base protocol include:

  • The frequency deviation of the subprotocol, given by fdf_d.

  • The symbol rate of the subprotocol relative to the symbol rate of the base protocol. This ratio is denoted NN and is given by

    N=T~sTsN=\frac{\tilde{T}_{s}}{T_{s}}(2.9)

  • The equivalent closed-loop bandwidth of the base protocol carrier phase PLL given by BnTsB_{n}T_{s}.

  • The value of Eb/N0E_{b}/N_{0} at which the base protocol operates.

These factors are examined below.

2.1.1 Signal Detection

The real-valued bandpass version of the received signal is

rbp(t)=Re{s(t)ej(2πf0t+ϕ(t))ejφ(t)}+w(t)r_{bp}(t)=\mathrm{Re}\{s(t)e^{j(2\pi f_{0}t+\phi(t))}e^{j\varphi(t)}\}+w(t)(2.10)

where φ(t)\varphi(t) is an unknown phase shift in addition to the phase induced by the subprotocol due to delay, oscillator uncertainty, or the Doppler shift. w(t)w(t) is the thermal noise modeled as a white wide-sense stationary normal random process with zero mean and power spectral density N0/2N_{0}/2 W/Hz.

A block diagram of the optimum (in the maximum likelihood sense) coherent detector is illustrated in Figure 2.1 (b). The received signal is downconverted and a filter is applied, matched to the base protocol pulse shape p(t)p(t). The matched filter output is sampled in synchronism with the symbols. (Perfect symbol timing synchronization is assumed, but not carrier phase synchronization. This is because signal samples produced by the carrier phase PLL for the base protocol are used to detect the subprotocol symbols.) The phase shift to be tracked by the base protocol’s carrier phase PLL is

θ(kTs)=ϕ(kTs)+φ(kTs)\theta(kT_{s})=\phi(kT_{s})+\varphi(kT_{s})(2.11)

The carrier phase PLL for the base protocol is shown by the blue blocks in the figure. The kk-th matched filter output x(kTs)x(kT_{s}) is de-rotated by the current phase estimate

θ^(kTs)=ϕ^(kTs)+φ^(kTs)\hat{\theta}(kT_{s})=\hat{\phi}(kT_{s})+\hat{\varphi}(kT_{s})(2.12)

The kk-th de-rotated matched filter output xr(kTs)x_{r}(kT_{s}) is used to make the kk-th symbol decision a^k\hat{a}_{k} for the base protocol. The de-rotated matched filter output xr(kTs)x_{r}(kT_{s}) and the decision a^k\hat{a}_{k} are used to compute the kk-th phase error using the maximum likelihood phase error detector (PED):

e(kTs)=Im{xr(kTs)a^k*}e(kT_{s})=\mathrm{Im}\{x_{r}(kT_{s})\hat{a}_{k}^{*}\}(2.13)

The kk-th error signal is filtered by the loop filter with z-domain transfer function F(z)F(z) whose output v(kTs)v(kT_{s}) drives a direct digital synthesizer (DDS). The DDS produces the next phase offset estimate θ^((k+1)Ts)\hat{\theta}((k+1)T_{s}) as described in [23].

The subprotocol detector is identified by the red blocks in Figure 2.1 (b). The input to the subprotocol detector is the loop filter output v(kTs)v(kT_{s}). Why this is the case is explained in the tracking analysis below where it is shown that v(kTs)v(kT_{s}) is a sampled version of a constant scale factor times the pulse train (2.4), where the sample rate is NN samples/symbol. Motivated by the optimum detector for PAM in the additive white Gaussian noise channel, v(kTs)v(kT_{s}) is applied to a filter matched to the subprotocol pulse shape p~(t)\tilde{p}(t). The matched filter output is “sampled” in synchronism with the symbols by retaining every NN-th sample. The sampled matched filter output is used to make symbol decisions.

2.2 PLL Analysis

To analyze the performance of a carrier-phase PLL in the presence of the subprotocol, we first examine the variance of the phase estimate θ^(kTs)\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}), which quantifies how much the PLL output fluctuates due to noise and other signal impairments. We will then introduce the effect of the subprotocol as one of such impairments. The limits on the PLL’s correction capability determine both the primary protocol’s bit error rate and the secondary channel’s signal-to-noise ratio, and thus the ability of the two protocols to coexist.

Establishing coexistence reveals a balancing act. As the frequency deviation of the subprotocol increases, the PLL loses its ability to track the induced phase variations, degrading performance in the primary link. While the subprotocol link is strengthened, it too breaks down as the PLL loses lock. Conversely, if the frequency deviation of the subprotocol is too small, the subprotocol symbols cannot be reliably decoded.

Assuming the primary protocol’s pulse shape satisfies the Nyquist no-ISI condition, the kk-th matched filter output is

x(kTs)=akejθ(kTs)+ν(kTs)x(kT_{s})=a_{k}e^{j\theta(kT_{s})}+\nu(kT_{s})(2.14)

where ν(kTs)\nu(kT_{s}) is a sequence of complex-valued normal random variables with zero mean and auto-correlation function

E{ν((k+m)Ts)ν*(kTs)}=2N0δK(m)E\{\nu((k+m)T_{s})\nu^{*}(kT_{s})\}=2N_{0}\delta_{K}(m)(2.15)

where δK(m)\delta_{K}(m) is the Kronecker delta function. The corresponding de-rotated matched filter output is

xr(kTs)=e−jθ^(kTs)x(kTs)x_{r}(kT_{s}) = e^{-j\hat{\theta}(kT_{s})}x(kT_{s})(2.16)
xr(kTs)=akej(θ(kTs)−θ^(kTs))+e−jθ^(kTs)ν(kTs)\phantom{x_{r}(kT_{s})} = a_{k}e^{j(\theta(kT_{s})-\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}))}+e^{-j\hat{\theta}(kT_{s})}\nu(kT_{s})(2.17)

The second term on the right-hand side of (2.17) is a complex-valued normal random variable with zero mean and autocorrelation function (2.15). Using (2.17), the kk-th PED output may be written

e(kTs)=Im{(akej(θ(kTs)−θ^(kTs))+e−jθ^(kTs)ν(kTs))a^k*}e(kT_{s}) = \mathrm{Im}\{(a_{k}e^{j(\theta(kT_{s})-\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}))}+e^{-j\hat{\theta}(kT_{s})}\nu(kT_{s}))\hat{a}_{k}^{*}\}(2.18)
e(kTs)=Im{aka^k*ej(θ(kTs)−θ^(kTs))+a^k*e−jθ^(kTs)ν(kTs)}\phantom{e(kT_{s})} = \mathrm{Im}\{a_{k}\hat{a}_{k}^{*}e^{j(\theta(kT_{s})-\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}))}+\hat{a}_{k}^{*}e^{-j\hat{\theta}(kT_{s})}\nu(kT_{s})\}(2.19)

Assuming the phase error θ(kTs)−θ^(kTs)\theta(kT_{s})-\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}) is small enough so that the decisions are correct (this assumption is justified in Section 2.2.1), the kk-th error sample becomes

e(kTs)=|ak|2Im{ej(θ(kTs)−θ^(kTs))}+Im{a^k*e−jθ^(kTs)ν(kTs)}e(kT_{s}) = |a_{k}|^{2}\mathrm{Im}\{e^{j(\theta(kT_{s})-\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}))}\}+\mathrm{Im}\{\hat{a}_{k}^{*}e^{-j\hat{\theta}(kT_{s})}\nu(kT_{s})\}(2.20)
e(kTs)=|ak|2sin(θ(kTs)−θ^(kTs))+ν0(kTs)\phantom{e(kT_{s})} = |a_{k}|^{2}\sin(\theta(kT_{s})-\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}))+\nu_{0}(kT_{s})(2.21)

In (2.21), the kk-th phase error is

θe(kTs)=θ(kTs)−θ^(kTs)\theta_{e}(kT_{s})=\theta(kT_{s})-\hat{\theta}(kT_{s})(2.22)

and the thermal noise term ν0(kTs)\nu_{0}(kT_{s}), which is the imaginary part of the de-rotated matched filter noise projected onto the symbol decision, is the kk-th member of a real-valued normal random sequence with zero mean and autocorrelation function

Rν0(m)=E{ν0((k+m)Ts)ν0(kTs)}=EavgN0δK(m)R_{\nu_{0}}(m)=E\{\nu_{0}((k+m)T_{s})\nu_{0}(kT_{s})\}=E_{avg}N_{0}\delta_{K}(m)(2.23)

The S-curve of the maximum likelihood PED is defined by [25]

g(θe)=E{e(kTs)|θe(kTs)=θe}g(\theta_{e})=E\{e(kT_{s})|\theta_{e}(kT_{s})=\theta_{e}\}(2.24)

where the expectation in (2.24) is with respect to the data symbols and the thermal noise. The S-curve for the data-aided version of the maximum likelihood PED is

g(θe)=Eavgsin(θe)g(\theta_{e})=E_{avg}\sin(\theta_{e})(2.25)

The S-curve (2.25) indicates there is one stable lock point and that the lock point is at θe=0\theta_{e}=0. For the decision-directed case, the S-curve exhibits multiple stable lock points that are determined by the rotational symmetries of the alphabet AA. Of interest in the tracking analysis below is the fact that for θe\theta_{e} near 0, the S-curves for the data-aided and decision-directed maximum likelihood PEDs coincide [23], [25].

The PED gain is the slope of the S-curve at the origin:

Kp=ddθeg(θe)|θe=0=EavgK_{p}=\frac{d}{d\theta_{e}}g(\theta_{e})|_{\theta_{e}=0}=E_{avg}(2.26)

The PED gain KpK_{p} is important in computing the loop filter coefficients to achieve a desired performance goal. The PED output (2.21) defines the system shown in Figure 2.2 (a). Following convention, a normalized version of the nonlinear S-curve is applied to the phase error. For this reason, the thermal noise term in the model is added before the application of the PED gain KpK_{p}. The relationship between ν1(kTs)\nu_{1}(kT_{s}) in Figure 2.2 (a) and the thermal noise term ν0(kTs)\nu_{0}(kT_{s}) in (2.21) is

ν1(kTs)=ν0(kTs)Kp\nu_{1}(kT_{s})=\frac{\nu_{0}(kT_{s})}{K_{p}}(2.27)

The sequence e(kTs)e(kT_{s}) is applied to the loop filter with transfer function F(z)F(z) whose output v(kTs)v(kT_{s}) is applied to a discrete-time integrator with transfer function z−1/(1−z−1)z^{-1}/(1-z^{-1}). The discrete-time integrator represents the phase accumulator in the DDS [23].

2.2.1 PLL Tracking Analysis

We now quantify the variance of the estimate θ^(kTs)\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}) in the lock condition. The variance of θ^(kTs)\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}) is the phase jitter of the system. The PLL is considered locked when θe(kTs)≈0\theta_{e}(kT_{s})\approx0. When θe(kTs)=0\theta_{e}(kT_{s})=0, the nonlinear abstraction in Figure 2.2 (a) may be replaced by the linear model in Figure 2.2 (b). The linear model permits the use of frequency-domain techniques in the analysis. The loop filter output v(kTs)v(kT_{s}) is of the form

v(kTs)=θ2(kTs)+ν2(kTs)v(kT_{s})=\theta_{2}(kT_{s})+\nu_{2}(kT_{s})(2.28)

where θ2(kTs)\theta_{2}(kT_{s}) is the contribution to v(kTs)v(kT_{s}) from θ(kTs)\theta(kT_{s}) and ν2(kTs)\nu_{2}(kT_{s}) is the contribution to v(kTs)v(kT_{s}) from ν1(kTs)\nu_{1}(kT_{s}). The z-transform of (2.28) is

V(z)=H2(z)Θ(z)+H2(z)N1(z)V(z)=H_{2}(z)\Theta(z)+H_{2}(z)N_{1}(z)(2.29)

where

H2(z)=Kp(1−z−1)F(z)1−z−1[1−KpF(z)]H_{2}(z)=\frac{K_{p}(1-z^{-1})F(z)}{1-z^{-1}[1-K_{p}F(z)]}(2.30)

Θ(z)\Theta(z) is the z-transform of θ(kTs)\theta(kT_{s}), and N1(z)N_{1}(z) is the z-transform of the realization of ν1(kTs)\nu_{1}(kT_{s}). The output θ^(kTs)\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}) is of the form

θ^(kTs)=θ3(kTs)+ν3(kTs)\hat{\theta}(kT_{s})=\theta_{3}(kT_{s})+\nu_{3}(kT_{s})(2.31)

where θ3(kTs)\theta_{3}(kT_{s}) is the contribution to θ^(kTs)\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}) due to θ(kTs)\theta(kT_{s}) and ν3(kTs)\nu_{3}(kT_{s}) is the contribution to θ^(kTs)\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}) due to ν1(kTs)\nu_{1}(kT_{s}). On a realization-by-realization basis, the z-transform of the loop output is

Θ^(z)=H3(z)Θ(z)+H3(z)N1(z)\hat{\Theta}(z)=H_{3}(z)\Theta(z)+H_{3}(z)N_{1}(z)(2.32)

where

H3(z)=Kpz−1F(z)1−z−1[1−KpF(z)]H_{3}(z)=\frac{K_{p}z^{-1}F(z)}{1-z^{-1}[1-K_{p}F(z)]}(2.33)

Θ(z)\Theta(z) is the z-transform of θ(kTs)\theta(kT_{s}), and N1(z)N_{1}(z) is the z-transform of the realization of ν1(kTs)\nu_{1}(kT_{s}).

The several noise terms introduced above all describe the same physical thermal noise, but observed at different points in the loop. We will later adapt this term to include noise induced by the subprotocol. For clarity, these noise terms thus far are summarized here:

  • ν(kTs)\nu(kT_{s}) is the complex-valued noise at the matched filter output, defined in (2.14);

  • ν0(kTs)\nu_{0}(kT_{s}) is the real-valued noise ν(kTs)\nu(kT_{s}) produces at the PED output (2.21), formed from the imaginary part of the de-rotated matched filter noise;

  • ν1(kTs)\nu_{1}(kT_{s}) is that same noise referred to the loop input, scaled by the PED gain KpK_{p} as described by (2.27); it is the noise injected into the linear model of Figure 2.2 (b);

  • ν2(kTs)\nu_{2}(kT_{s}) is the noise component of the loop filter output v(kTs)v(kT_{s}), equal to the response of ν1(kTs)\nu_{1}(kT_{s}) through H2(z)H_{2}(z);

  • ν3(kTs)\nu_{3}(kT_{s}) is the noise component of the phase estimate θ^(kTs)\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}), equal to the response of ν1(kTs)\nu_{1}(kT_{s}) through H3(z)H_{3}(z).

The performance of the base protocol is a function of the phase jitter. As shown above, the variance of θ^(kTs)\hat{\theta}(kT_{s}) is the variance of the noise term ν3(kTs)\nu_{3}(kT_{s}) which is obtained as follows. From (2.23) and (2.27), the autocorrelation function of ν1(kTs)\nu_{1}(kT_{s}) is

Rν1(m)=EavgN0Kp2δK(m)R_{\nu_{1}}(m)=\frac{E_{avg}N_{0}}{K_{p}^{2}}\delta_{K}(m)(2.34)

By the Wiener-Khinchin Theorem, the power spectral density of ν1(kTs)\nu_{1}(kT_{s}) is

Sν1(ejΩ)=EavgN0Kp2S_{\nu_{1}}(e^{j\Omega})=\frac{E_{avg}N_{0}}{K_{p}^{2}}(2.35)

From (2.32), ν3(kTs)\nu_{3}(kT_{s}) is the response to input ν1(kTs)\nu_{1}(kT_{s}) by a system with transfer function H3(z)H_{3}(z). Consequently, the power spectral density of ν3(kTs)\nu_{3}(kT_{s}) is

Sν3(ejΩ)=EavgN0Kp2|H3(ejΩ)|2S_{\nu_{3}}(e^{j\Omega})=\frac{E_{avg}N_{0}}{K_{p}^{2}}|H_{3}(e^{j\Omega})|^{2}(2.36)

The variance of ν3(kTs)\nu_{3}(kT_{s}) is

σν32=12π∫−ππSν3(ejΩ)dΩ=EavgN0Kp212π∫−ππ|H3(ejΩ)|2dΩ\sigma_{\nu_{3}}^{2}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}S_{\nu_{3}}(e^{j\Omega})\,d\Omega=\frac{E_{avg}N_{0}}{K_{p}^{2}}\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|H_{3}(e^{j\Omega})|^{2}\,d\Omega(2.37)

The closed-loop equivalent noise bandwidth is defined by [23], [25]

BnTs=14π∫−ππ|H3(ejΩ)|2dΩ.B_{n}T_{s}=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|H_{3}(e^{j\Omega})|^{2}\,d\Omega.(2.38)

Using (2.26) and this definition, the variance σν32\sigma_{\nu_{3}}^{2} may be written

σν32=2BnTsEavg/N0\sigma_{\nu_{3}}^{2}=\frac{2B_{n}T_{s}}{E_{avg}/N_{0}}(2.39)

The relationship (2.39) shows that the phase jitter for the base protocol is proportional to the closed loop bandwidth and inversely proportional to Eavg/N0E_{avg}/N_{0}. For a given Eavg/N0E_{avg}/N_{0}, decreasing BnTsB_{n}T_{s} reduces phase jitter (which is desirable), but it also increases acquisition time (undesirable) and reduces the pull-in range (also undesirable). The carrier phase PLL used in the base protocol selects BnTsB_{n}T_{s} to balance these competing effects and achieve an acceptable overall trade-off.

2.2.2 Subprotocol Performance

With the loop carrier phase PLL designed to meet the performance requirements of the base protocol, what is the impact on the subprotocol? We return to (2.29) and a close examination of (2.30). For large NN and small fdf_{d}, the pulse train representing the base protocol is highly oversampled. Consequently, our interest is in the behavior of the frequency response H2(ejΩ)H_{2}(e^{j\Omega}) for Ω\Omega near 0. Using the first-order Taylor series approximation

e−jΩ≈1−jΩe^{-j\Omega}\approx1-j\Omega(2.40)

for Ω≈0\Omega\approx0, the frequency response H2(ejΩ)H_{2}(e^{j\Omega}) for Ω\Omega near zero is

H2(ejΩ)≈jΩH_{2}(e^{j\Omega})\approx j\Omega(2.41)

In words, H2(z)H_{2}(z) acts as a differentiator for highly oversampled inputs. Thus, assuming the highly oversampled condition, the phase component θ2(kTs)\theta_{2}(kT_{s}) in (2.28) is

θ2(kTs)≈θ′(kTs)\theta_{2}(kT_{s}) \approx \theta'(kT_{s})(2.42)
θ2(kTs)≈ϕ′(kTs)+φ′(kTs)\phantom{\theta_{2}(kT_{s})} \approx \phi'(kT_{s})+\varphi'(kT_{s})(2.43)
θ2(kTs)≈2πfd∑k~=−∞∞a~k~p~(kTs−k~T~s)+φ′(kTs)\phantom{\theta_{2}(kT_{s})} \approx 2\pi f_{d}\sum_{\tilde{k}=-\infty}^{\infty}\tilde{a}_{\tilde{k}}\tilde{p}(kT_{s}-\tilde{k}\tilde{T}_{s})+\varphi'(kT_{s})(2.44)

where we differentiate (2.7) to obtain (2.44).

The approximation (2.41), and with it (2.44), is not unconditional. It holds only while the bandwidth of the subprotocol pulse train lies below the closed-loop bandwidth of the base protocol’s carrier phase PLL. Outside that condition the loop no longer presents a flat differentiator to the subprotocol; it attenuates and disperses the pulse train instead, and (2.44) ceases to describe v(kTs)v(kT_{s}) at all. Since the pulse train occupies roughly (1+β)/2T~s(1+\beta)/2\tilde{T}_{s} and the loop passes roughly BnTsB_{n}T_{s} cycles per base-protocol symbol, the condition is a lower bound on NN. This is a separate failure mode from the loss of lock analyzed below: here the base protocol is untouched and it is the subprotocol that fails, because the observable it is read from has been filtered away. Chapter 3 shows that this bound produces a notably abrupt edge in the measured operating region.

The first term on the right-hand side of (2.44) corresponds to a sampled version of the scaled pulse train in (2.4), allowing us to recover the subprotocol symbols with a second matched filter. The associated scaling factor is proportional to the frequency deviation fdf_d.

The second term on the right-hand side of (2.44) corresponds to a sampled version of the time derivative of the channel-induced phase, which is the noise term of the subprotocol. This term can be interpreted under three representative cases:

  1. The phase offset is constant, i.e., φ(t)=const\varphi(t)=\text{const}. In this case, φ′(kTs)=0\varphi'(kT_s)=0.

  2. The phase offset is a linear ramp, φ(t)=2πΔft\varphi(t)=2\pi \Delta f\, t, corresponding to a constant frequency offset of Δf\Delta f (cycles/s) at the PLL input. In order to track a constant frequency offset with zero steady-state phase error, the loop filter must include a pole at z=1z=1 [23]. A proportional-plus-integral loop filter is therefore typically employed [23]. In this case, φ′(kTs)=2πΔf\varphi'(kT_s)=2\pi \Delta f which is constant and, when normalized per symbol interval, scales as 2πΔfTs2\pi \Delta f T_s. This term depends on the ratio between the frequency offset and the symbol rate of the base protocol. For practical carrier phase-locked loops, negligible performance degradation typically requires ΔfTs≲0.01\Delta f T_s \lesssim 0.01 [25]. Accordingly, this contribution is generally small and may be suppressed in practice by applying a DC-blocking filter to v(kTs)v(kT_s) prior to detection.

  3. The phase offset is time-varying in a more general sense. If φ′(kTs)\varphi'(kT_s) is not constant, the subprotocol remains valid provided that the variation of φ′(kTs)\varphi'(kT_s) is slow relative to the subprotocol symbol rate.

A changing Doppler shift also provides negligible disturbance for the subprotocol. Consider a platform closing at 300300 m/s with a 11 km miss distance at a 915915 MHz carrier. The Doppler shift sweeps most rapidly at closest approach, at approximately

|dfDdt|≈v2λd≈270Hz/s\left|\frac{d f_{D}}{dt}\right|\approx\frac{v^{2}}{\lambda d}\approx270~\text{Hz/s}(2.45)

where vv is the closing speed, λ\lambda the carrier wavelength, and dd the miss distance. Over a single subprotocol symbol—tens of microseconds for the parameters used in this work—the Doppler shift changes by a few millihertz, which is negligible beside the deviation fdA~f_{d}\tilde{A} the subprotocol itself imposes. The channel term φ′(kTs)\varphi'(kT_{s}) in (2.44) is thus orders of magnitude below the subprotocol term for realistic geometries, and whatever residual constant remains is removed by the DC blocker in any case.

The regime that does defeat this argument is high mobility combined with fast frequency-selective fading, in which φ(t)\varphi(t) ceases to be quasi-static and Case 3 no longer applies. That case is the principal limitation of the technique, and Chapter 3 examines it directly under the ITU delay profiles.

In light of the common case number 2 above, however, our analysis uses the proportional-plus-integrator loop filter [23]

F(z)=K1+K21−z−1F(z)=K_{1}+\frac{K_{2}}{1-z^{-1}}(2.46)

to create a second-order closed-loop response with BnTs=0.02B_{n}T_{s}=0.02 cycles/symbol with an equivalent s-domain damping factor ζ=1/2\zeta=1/\sqrt{2}, the same values used for the lock limits of Figure 2.5 and for every simulation in Chapter 3.b The two frequency responses H2(ej2πF)H_{2}(e^{j2\pi F}) and H3(ej2πF)H_{3}(e^{j2\pi F}) are plotted in Figure 2.3. Observe that for F in the vicinity of 0, H2(ej2πF)H_{2}(e^{j2\pi F}) approximates the ideal derivative jΩ=j2πFj\Omega=j2\pi F which is the desired behavior for subprotocol symbol estimation.

b The design used the continuous-time to discrete-time transformation outlined in Appendix C of [23].

To estimate the noise of the loop filter output in the presence of the subprotocol, we revisit (2.28), where ν2(kTs)\nu_{2}(kT_{s}) is seen to be the response to ν1(kTs)\nu_{1}(kT_{s}) of a system with frequency response H2(ejΩ)H_{2}(e^{j\Omega}). Consequently, the power spectral density of the sequence ν2(kTs)\nu_{2}(kT_{s}) is

Sν2(ejΩ)=EavgN0Kp2|H2(ejΩ)|2S_{\nu_{2}}(e^{j\Omega})=\frac{E_{avg}N_{0}}{K_{p}^{2}}|H_{2}(e^{j\Omega})|^{2}(2.47)

The noise sample in (2.28) is the kk-th member of a correlated random sequence of zero-mean normal random variables. The system shown in Figure 2.1 (b) uses a non-optimal reduced-complexity detectorc but one that is still optimum in the case of white noise. The noise variance under such a detector is

c The true optimum detector (in the maximum likelihood sense) for a pulse train in correlated noise is discussed in Chapter 9 of [24].
σν22=12π∫−ππSν2(ejΩ)dΩ=EavgN0Kp212π∫−ππ|H2(ejΩ)|2dΩ\sigma_{\nu_{2}}^{2}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}S_{\nu_{2}}(e^{j\Omega})\,d\Omega=\frac{E_{avg}N_{0}}{K_{p}^{2}}\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|H_{2}(e^{j\Omega})|^{2}\,d\Omega(2.48)

The corresponding variances σν22\sigma_{\nu_{2}}^{2} and σν32\sigma_{\nu_{3}}^{2} are plotted in Figure 2.4.

We will now show that the probability of error for the subprotocol is a function of the primary protocol’s signal-to-noise ratio. An example is given for the binary case:

𝒜~={−A~,+A~}\tilde{\mathcal{A}}=\{-\tilde{A},+\tilde{A}\}(2.49)

Assuming the matched filter has unit energy and that the subprotocol pulse shape satisfies the Nyquist no-ISI condition, the k~\tilde{k}-th matched filter output is

x~(k~T~s)=2πfda~k~+ν~2\tilde{x}(\tilde{k}\tilde{T}_{s})=2\pi f_{d}\tilde{a}_{\tilde{k}}+\tilde{\nu}_{2}(2.50)

where ν~2\tilde{\nu}_{2} is a real-valued normal random variable with zero mean and variance

σν~22=σν22\sigma_{\tilde{\nu}_{2}}^{2}=\sigma_{\nu_{2}}^{2}(2.51)

The equality follows from the unit-energy assumption on p~(t)\tilde{p}(t), since the matched filter scales noise variance by the squared ℓ2\ell^2-norm of its coefficients.

The probability of error depends on the effective signal-to-noise ratio at the subprotocol matched filter output, given by

E~avgσν~22=(2πfdA~)2I2EavgN0\frac{\tilde{E}_{avg}}{\sigma_{\tilde{\nu}_{2}}^{2}}=\frac{(2\pi f_{d}\tilde{A})^{2}}{I_{2}}\frac{E_{avg}}{N_{0}}(2.52)

where I2I_{2} is the integral on the right-hand side of (2.48). The numerator (2πfdA~)2(2\pi f_d \tilde{A})^2 is the squared signal amplitude at the subprotocol detector input, determined entirely by the frequency deviation fdf_d and symbol amplitude A~\tilde{A}. The denominator I2⋅N0/EavgI_2 \cdot N_0 / E_{avg} is the noise variance σν~22\sigma_{\tilde{\nu}_2}^2 at that same input, which depends on N0N_0 and the equivalent noise bandwidth of the base protocol’s carrier phase PLL through I2I_2. Crucially, the subprotocol SNR scales linearly with the base protocol’s Eavg/N0E_{avg}/N_0: a stronger primary link directly improves secondary channel reliability. This coupling means the subprotocol effectively borrows SNR from the primary link rather than having an independent noise budget.

2.2.3 Lock Limits

The ability of the base protocol’s carrier phase PLL to track out the phase induced by the subprotocol is the limiting factor for fdA~.f_{d}\tilde{A}. Gardner examined “modulation limits” for the case where the input is an FM signal modulated by m(t)m(t) [26]. Two cases for m(t)m(t) are considered.

Case 1: Sinusoidal Modulation In the case of sinusoidal modulation, the modulating signal is

m(t)=Apeaksin(ωmt)m(t) = A_{peak} \sin(\omega_m t)(2.53)

The peak frequency deviation is fdApeakf_{d}A_{peak}. For a second-order PLL, the peak frequency deviation must satisfy

fdApeak<ωn22πωm,ωm≪ωnf_{d}A_{peak}<\frac{\omega_{n}^{2}}{2\pi\omega_{m}}, \quad \omega_{m}\ll\omega_{n}(2.54)

The following steps are used to apply this result to the current problem:

  1. Multiplying both sides of (2.54) by TsT_{s} normalizes the peak frequency deviation to the base protocol symbol time:

    fdApeakTs<ωn2Ts2πωm,ωm≪ωnf_{d}A_{peak}T_{s}<\frac{\omega_{n}^{2}T_{s}}{2\pi\omega_{m}}, \quad \omega_{m}\ll\omega_{n}(2.55)

  2. For the proportional-plus-integrator loop filter, the natural frequency ωn\omega_{n} and equivalent noise bandwidth BnB_n are related by

    Bn=ωn2(ζ+14ζ)⇒ωn=2Bn(ζ+14ζ)B_{n}=\frac{\omega_{n}}{2}\!\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)\Rightarrow\omega_{n}=\frac{2B_{n}}{\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)}(2.56)

    Substituting (2.56) into (2.55) produces

    fdApeakTs<4Bn2Ts2πωm(ζ+14ζ)2,ωm≪2Bn(ζ+14ζ)f_{d}A_{peak}T_{s}<\frac{4B_{n}^{2}T_{s}}{2\pi\omega_{m}\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)^{2}}, \quad \omega_{m}\ll \frac{2B_{n}}{\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)}(2.57)

  3. The period of the sinusoid is the symbol time for the subprotocol:

    ωm=2πT~s\omega_{m}=\frac{2\pi}{\tilde{T}_{s}}(2.58)

    Substituting (2.58) into (2.57) produces

    fdApeakTs<4Bn2TsT~s(2π)2(ζ+14ζ)2,2πT~s<2Bn(ζ+14ζ)f_{d}A_{peak}T_{s}<\frac{4B_{n}^{2}T_{s}\tilde{T}_{s}}{(2\pi)^{2}\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)^{2}}, \quad \frac{2\pi}{\tilde{T}_{s}}<\frac{2B_{n}}{\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)}(2.59)

  4. For binary PAM with 𝒜~={−A~,+A~}\tilde{\mathcal{A}}=\{-\tilde{A},+\tilde{A}\}, an alternating symbol sequence produces an approximate sinusoid with peak amplitude

    Apeak=A~p~peakA_{peak}=\tilde{A}\tilde{p}_{peak}(2.60)

    where

    p~peak=∑k~=−∞∞(−1)k~p~(k~T~s)\tilde{p}_{peak}=\sum_{\tilde{k}=-\infty}^{\infty}(-1)^{\tilde{k}}\tilde{p}(\tilde{k}\tilde{T}_{s})(2.61)

    If p~(t)\tilde{p}(t) is the square-root raised-cosine pulse shape with roll-off β\beta, normalized as above to unity DC gain, then

    p~peak=∑k~=−∞∞(−1)k~sin(π(1−β)k~)+4βk~cos(π(1+β)k~)πk~[1−(4βk~)2]=κ\tilde{p}_{peak}=\sum_{\tilde{k}=-\infty}^{\infty}(-1)^{\tilde{k}}\frac{\sin(\pi(1-\beta)\tilde{k})+4\beta \tilde{k}\cos(\pi(1+\beta)\tilde{k})}{\pi \tilde{k}[1-(4\beta \tilde{k})^{2}]}=\kappa(2.62)

    where κ≈0.1414\kappa\approx0.1414 is essentially independent of β\beta. Substituting (2.62) into (2.59) produces

    fdA~Tsκ<4Bn2TsT~s(2π)2(ζ+14ζ)2,2πT~s<2Bn(ζ+14ζ)f_{d}\tilde{A}T_{s}\kappa<\frac{4B_{n}^{2}T_{s}\tilde{T}_{s}}{(2\pi)^{2}\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)^{2}}, \quad \frac{2\pi}{\tilde{T}_{s}}<\frac{2B_{n}}{\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)}(2.63)

  5. Simplify using T~s/Ts=N\tilde{T}_{s}/T_{s}=N:

    fdA~Tsκ<(BnTs)2Nπ2(ζ+14ζ)2,N≫πBnTs(ζ+14ζ)f_{d}\tilde{A}T_{s}\kappa<\frac{(B_{n}T_{s})^{2}N}{\pi^{2}\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)^{2}}, \quad N\gg\frac{\pi}{B_{n}T_{s}}\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)(2.64)

The final result is that the following relationship must be satisfied for the carrier phase PLL to maintain lock during tracking:

fdA~Ts(BnTs)2Nκ<1π2(ζ+14ζ)2,N≫πBnTs(ζ+14ζ)\frac{f_{d}\tilde{A}T_{s}}{(B_{n}T_{s})^{2}N}\kappa<\frac{1}{\pi^{2}\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)^{2}}, \quad N\gg\frac{\pi}{B_{n}T_{s}}\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)(2.65)

Case 2: Random Modulation In this case m(t)m(t) is a wide-sense stationary Gaussian random process with zero mean and power spectral density

Sm(f)={constant|f|<Bm0otherwise.S_{m}(f)=\begin{cases}\text{constant}&|f|<B_{m}\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}(2.66)

The Gaussian random process creates an RMS frequency deviation of σf\sigma_{f} in the modulated carrier. The ability of a PLL to track the instantaneous phase places an upper limit, called a “lock limit,” on the RMS frequency deviation. The lock limit for a second-order PLL is [26, Eq. (5.23)]

σf<3ωn24π2γBm,Bm≪ωn2π\sigma_{f}<\frac{\sqrt{3}\omega_{n}^{2}}{4\pi^{2}\gamma B_{m}}, \quad B_{m}\ll\frac{\omega_{n}}{2\pi}(2.67)

where γ\gamma is an experimentally determined constant called a “crest factor” in [26]. The following steps are used to apply this result to the current problem:

  1. The RMS frequency deviation relative to the sample time (== the symbol time of the base protocol) is the desired quantity. Multiplying both sides of (2.67) by TsT_{s} produces

    σfTs<3ωn2Ts4π2γBm,Bm≪ωn2π\sigma_{f}T_{s}<\frac{\sqrt{3}\omega_{n}^{2}T_{s}}{4\pi^{2}\gamma B_{m}}, \quad B_{m}\ll\frac{\omega_{n}}{2\pi}(2.68)

    σfTs<34Bn2Ts4π2γBm(ζ+14ζ)2,Bm<2Bn2π(ζ+14ζ)\sigma_{f}T_{s}<\frac{\sqrt{3}\,4B_{n}^{2}T_{s}}{4\pi^{2}\gamma B_{m}\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)^{2}}, \quad B_{m}<\frac{2B_{n}}{2\pi\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)}(2.69)

    Bm=1+β2T~sB_{m}=\frac{1+\beta}{2\tilde{T}_{s}}(2.70)

    Substituting (2.70) into (2.69) produces

    σfTs<83Bn2TsT~s4π2γ(1+β)(ζ+14ζ)2,1+β2T~s≪2Bn2π(ζ+14ζ)\sigma_{f}T_{s}<\frac{8\sqrt{3}B_{n}^{2}T_{s}\tilde{T}_{s}}{4\pi^{2}\gamma(1+\beta)\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)^{2}}, \quad \frac{1+\beta}{2\tilde{T}_{s}}\ll\frac{2B_{n}}{2\pi\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)}(2.71)

    σf=fd×RMS value of s~(t)\sigma_{f}=f_{d}\times \text{RMS value of } \tilde{s}(t)(2.73)

    For a pulse shape normalized to unity DC gain that satisfies the Nyquist no-ISI condition, the RMS value of s~(t)\tilde{s}(t) is

    RMS value of s~(t)=ρE~avg,ρ=1\text{RMS value of } \tilde{s}(t)=\rho\sqrt{\tilde{E}_{avg}},\qquad \rho=1(2.74)

    where, as with κ\kappa in (2.62), the unity-DC-gain normalization leaves ρ\rho a pure number independent of both β\beta and T~s\tilde{T}_{s}. For M~=2\tilde{M}=2, 𝒜~={−A~,+A~}\tilde{\mathcal{A}}=\{-\tilde{A},+\tilde{A}\} so that E~avg=A~2\tilde{E}_{avg}=\tilde{A}^{2}. Thus,

    RMS value of s~(t)=A~\text{RMS value of } \tilde{s}(t)=\tilde{A}(2.75)

    which is simply the statement that an iid binary subprotocol sequence drives the carrier to ±fdA~\pm f_{d}\tilde{A} Hz. Substituting (2.75) into (2.73) produces

    σf=fdA~\sigma_{f}=f_{d}\tilde{A}(2.76)
