    fdA~Tsρ<23π2γ(1+β)(ζ+14ζ)2(BnTs)2Nf_{d}\tilde{A}T_{s}\rho<\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{\pi^{2}\gamma(1+\beta)\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)^{2}}\,(B_{n}T_{s})^{2}N(2.77)

The final result is that the following relationship must be satisfied for the carrier phase PLL to maintain lock during tracking:

fdA~Ts(BnTs)2Nρ<23π2γ(1+β)(ζ+14ζ)2,N≫π(1+β)2(BnTs)(ζ+14ζ)\frac{f_{d}\tilde{A}T_{s}}{(B_{n}T_{s})^{2}N}\rho<\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{\pi^{2}\gamma(1+\beta)\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)^{2}}, \quad N\gg\frac{\pi(1+\beta)}{2(B_{n}T_{s})}\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)(2.78)

Summary The two lock limits (2.65) for sinusoidal modulation and (2.78) for random modulation are not merely similar; under the unity-DC-gain normalization they are the same inequality with different constants. Both bound the ratio

fdA~Ts(BnTs)2N\frac{f_{d}\tilde{A}T_{s}}{(B_{n}T_{s})^{2}N}(2.79)

and both impose a loose lower bound on NN, so the pair may be collapsed into the single common form

fdA~Ts(BnTs)2Nc<Cπ2(ζ+14ζ)2,N≫πBnTs(ζ+14ζ)\frac{f_{d}\tilde{A}T_{s}}{\left(B_{n}T_{s}\right)^{2}N}\,c<\frac{C}{\pi^{2}\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)^{2}}, \qquad N\gg\frac{\pi}{B_{n}T_{s}}\left(\zeta+\frac{1}{4\zeta}\right)(2.80)

with

(c,C)={(κ,1)sinusoidal modulation(ρ,23γ(1+β))random modulation(c,C)=\begin{cases} (\kappa,\;1) & \text{sinusoidal modulation}\\[2pt] \left(\rho,\;\dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{\gamma(1+\beta)}\right) & \text{random modulation} \end{cases}(2.81)

where κ≈0.1414\kappa\approx0.1414 from (2.62) and ρ=1\rho=1 from (2.74). The constants cc are the pulse-shape amplitude normalizations; the constants CC carry the difference between the two modulation models. For the random case the lower bound on NN acquires a factor (1+β)/2(1+\beta)/2, which for the β=1\beta=1 pulse used throughout this work leaves the two conditions identical. The lock limit for random modulation is tighter than that for sinusoidal modulation when

γ(1+β)>23κρ≈0.49\gamma(1+\beta)>\frac{2\sqrt{3}\,\kappa}{\rho}\approx0.49(2.82)

Gardner explains that γ=3.5\gamma=3.5 “has been found as a good empirical fit to laboratory observations on modulation unlock” [26]. Using this value of γ\gamma with β=1\beta=1 gives γ(1+β)=7\gamma(1+\beta)=7, so (2.82) is amply satisfied and the random-modulation limit is the more conservative of the two in this application. The two limits differ by a factor of γ(1+β)ρ/(23κ)≈14.3\gamma(1+\beta)\rho/(2\sqrt{3}\kappa)\approx14.3, so together they bracket roughly one decade of admissible deviation. A plot of whether or not the conditions (2.65) and (2.78) are satisfied is shown in Figure 2.5 for binary PAM using the square-root raised-cosine pulse shape with β=1,\beta=1, and for BnTs=0.02B_{n}T_{s}=0.02 cycles/symbol, κ=0.1414\kappa=0.1414, ρ=1\rho=1, and γ=3.5\gamma=3.5.

Figure 2.5 aligns with intuitive expectations, demonstrating that the system cannot simultaneously support an excessively large frequency deviation and a high subprotocol rate. Instead, a fundamental trade-off governs these two parameters. Reducing the frequency deviation allows for a higher relative symbol rate in the subprotocol; however, as indicated by (2.52), this increased rate comes at the expense of degrading the signal-to-noise ratio at the subprotocol detector’s input. Conversely, employing a higher frequency deviation restricts the subprotocol to a lower relative symbol rate, but consequently improves the signal-to-noise ratio at the detector.

The subprotocol pulse train (2.4) is neither a sinusoid nor is it a Gaussian random process for equally likely, iid symbols. The subprotocol pulse train is “more random” than a sinusoid, but “less random” than the assumed Gaussian random process that led to the modulation bound (2.78). Consequently, one expects the FLE subprotocol to behave somewhere in between these two cases; the lock boundary is somewhere in the light-gray area in the figure. Chapter 3 measures this boundary directly.

2.2.4 Consequences of the Lock Limits

Taken together with the subprotocol signal-to-noise ratio (2.52), the common form (2.80) yields three observations about the shape of the resulting operating region, each of which is revisited against measurement in Chapter 3.

First, the maximum admissible normalized deviation grows linearly in NN. This is a direct consequence of the unity-DC-gain normalization: because the peak and RMS excursions of s~(t)\tilde{s}(t) are set by A~\tilde{A} alone and do not depend on T~s\tilde{T}_{s}, the only place the subprotocol symbol rate enters the bound is through the modulating frequency ωm∝1/T~s\omega_{m}\propto1/\tilde{T}_{s}. Halving the subprotocol rate halves the rate of change the loop must follow and therefore doubles the deviation it can absorb.

Second, and more consequentially for system design, the admissible deviation grows as (BnTs)2(B_{n}T_{s})^{2}. A receiver with a wider carrier tracking loop—which is the usual choice for robust operation under Doppler and oscillator uncertainty—admits quadratically more subprotocol capacity. The margin that FLE consumes is therefore not a fixed quantity but one that grows with the base protocol’s own robustness: the more defensively the primary link is engineered, the more room the subprotocol has to work in. A link designed for a benign channel leaves little for FLE to use, while one designed for a hostile one leaves a great deal.

Third, the two limits bound the answer from both sides but do not determine it, since the pulse train is neither of the two modulation models Gardner analyzed. The measured boundary is therefore expected to lie between them.

Finally, it is reasonable to ask why the same margin could not simply be reclaimed by narrowing the synchronization loop instead of overlaying a subprotocol on it. Equation (2.39) shows what that would buy. Reducing BnTsB_{n}T_{s} lowers the base protocol’s phase jitter, which yields a marginal bit error rate improvement; that improvement can be converted into throughput only by renegotiating the modulation and coding scheme with an associated peer, and it is paid for with longer acquisition time and a smaller pull-in range. FLE converts the same margin into bits that are legible to any receiver capable of estimating carrier frequency offset, whether or not that receiver is associated, keyed, or able to demodulate the payload at all. The two uses of the margin are therefore not interchangeable, and they are not even addressed to the same audience: narrowing the loop pays a dividend to the link that already exists, whereas FLE pays one to the links that do not.

2.3 Extension to Multi-Carrier

With the single-carrier system description in place, the multi-carrier system is straightforward to describe. The key conceptual difference is the mechanism the base protocol uses to estimate carrier frequency offset (CFO): a single-carrier receiver tracks the carrier phase continuously with a per-symbol PLL, whereas an orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) receiver estimates the CFO at most once per OFDM symbol, using either a dedicated preamble or embedded pilot subcarriers [27]–[29]. The FLE subprotocol attaches to whatever CFO observable the base protocol produces; the only change relative to the single-carrier model is the rate and the statistics of that observable.

2.3.1 Signal Model

Consider an OFDM base protocol with NcN_{c} active subcarriers, subcarrier spacing Δsc\Delta_{sc}, useful (IFFT) symbol duration Tu=1/ΔscT_{u}=1/\Delta_{sc}, and cyclic prefix (CP) duration TcpT_{cp}, so that the OFDM symbol duration is Tsym=Tu+TcpT_{sym}=T_{u}+T_{cp}. Let ai,na_{i,n} denote the constellation point applied to the nn-th subcarrier of the ii-th OFDM symbol. In place of the primary pulse train of the single-carrier model, the base protocol forms each OFDM symbol with the inverse FFT, producing the complex-valued lowpass equivalent waveform

s(t)=∑i=−∞∞∑n=0Nc−1ai,nej2πnΔsc(t−iTsym−Tcp)g(t−iTsym)s(t)=\sum_{i=-\infty}^{\infty}\sum_{n=0}^{N_{c}-1}a_{i,n}\,e^{j2\pi n\Delta_{sc}(t-iT_{sym}-T_{cp})}\,g(t-iT_{sym})(2.83)

where g(t)g(t) is the rectangular (or windowed) OFDM symbol-shaping pulse of duration TsymT_{sym} that includes the cyclic prefix. Exactly as in the single-carrier case (2.3), the FLE subprotocol perturbs the up-conversion with the subprotocol phase ϕ(t)\phi(t) of (2.6)–(2.8):

sbp(t)=Re{s(t)ej(2πf0t+ϕ(t))}.s_{bp}(t)=\mathrm{Re}\{s(t)e^{j(2\pi f_{0}t+\phi(t))}\}.(2.84)

To preserve subcarrier orthogonality, the residual frequency deviation seen within any single OFDM symbol must be small compared with the subcarrier spacing, i.e., fdA~≪Δscf_{d}\tilde{A}\ll\Delta_{sc}; otherwise the perturbation introduces inter-carrier interference (ICI) that degrades the base protocol [27], [30]. This is the multi-carrier analogue of the single-carrier requirement that the carrier phase PLL track ϕ(t)\phi(t) without significant degradation.

2.3.2 Detection

The OFDM detector differs fundamentally from the single-carrier detector. Detection is performed on blocks of received samples: the CP is discarded, the FFT of each block is computed, and primary symbol decisions are made on a subcarrier-by-subcarrier basis. A residual CFO δf\delta f that is constant over an OFDM symbol rotates the ii-th symbol’s subcarriers by a common phase 2πδf(t−iTsym)2\pi\,\delta f\,(t-iT_{sym}) and, to first order, scales each subcarrier by sinc(δfTu)\mathrm{sinc}(\delta f\,T_{u}) while leaking energy into adjacent subcarriers [30]. The base protocol estimates and removes this CFO; the resulting per-symbol CFO estimate is the observable from which the secondary data is recovered.

Let δf^i\widehat{\delta f}_{i} denote the CFO estimate produced for the ii-th OFDM symbol. Because the subprotocol phase varies slowly relative to the base-protocol carrier, δf^i\widehat{\delta f}_{i} is a sample of the instantaneous frequency 12πϕ′(t)\tfrac{1}{2\pi}\phi'(t) averaged over the ii-th OFDM symbol,

δf^i≈12πTsym[ϕ(iTsym)−ϕ((i−1)Tsym)]+ηi≈fd∑k~a~k~p~(iTsym−k~T~s)+ηi,\widehat{\delta f}_{i}\approx\frac{1}{2\pi T_{sym}}\big[\phi(iT_{sym})-\phi((i-1)T_{sym})\big]+\eta_{i} \approx f_{d}\sum_{\tilde{k}}\tilde{a}_{\tilde{k}}\tilde{p}(iT_{sym}-\tilde{k}\tilde{T}_{s})+\eta_{i},(2.85)

where ηi\eta_{i} is the frequency-estimation error. Comparing (2.85) with the single-carrier result (2.44), the per-OFDM-symbol CFO estimate plays exactly the role of the PLL loop-filter output v(kTs)v(kT_{s}): it is a scaled, noisy sample of the subprotocol pulse train (2.4), but now the sample period is the OFDM symbol duration TsymT_{sym} rather than the base-protocol symbol time TsT_{s}. The secondary detector therefore reuses the single-carrier structure: the sequence {δf^i}\{\widehat{\delta f}_{i}\} is applied to a filter matched to the subprotocol pulse shape p~(t)\tilde{p}(t) (now sampled at rate 1/Tsym1/T_{sym}) and decimated to the subprotocol symbol rate.

The consequence is a hard upper bound on the secondary symbol rate. Because a CFO estimate is available at most once per OFDM symbol, the maximum secondary symbol rate is one secondary symbol per OFDM symbol,

1T~s≤1Tsym,equivalentlyN=T~sTsym≥1.\frac{1}{\tilde{T}_{s}}\le\frac{1}{T_{sym}},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad N=\frac{\tilde{T}_{s}}{T_{sym}}\ge 1 .(2.86)

Here NN is reinterpreted as the number of OFDM symbols per secondary symbol, the multi-carrier counterpart of the oversampling ratio defined in (2.9). Two regimes of operation follow from how the base protocol produces its CFO estimates: a constant (continuous) transmission mode and a burst mode.

2.3.3 Constant (Continuous) Transmission Mode

In continuously transmitted, framed systems (e.g., the LTE/5G-NR downlink) the base protocol embeds reference (pilot) resource elements at a regular cadence and tracks residual CFO and phase noise across OFDM symbols [28], [31], [32]. Because transmission never stops, the phase ϕ(t)\phi(t) can be tracked with a PLL in exactly the manner analyzed in the single-carrier case, with one substitution: the error-signal update rate is set by the temporal spacing TpT_{p} of the pilots used to form the phase/frequency error, rather than by the base-protocol symbol time. All of the single-carrier tracking results carry over under the replacement Ts→TpT_{s}\rightarrow T_{p} (with Tp=TsymT_{p}=T_{sym} when every OFDM symbol carries pilots). In particular, the phase-jitter relationship (2.39) becomes

σθ^2=2BnTpEavg/N0,\sigma_{\hat{\theta}}^{2}=\frac{2B_{n}T_{p}}{E_{avg}/N_{0}},(2.87)

and the lock limits (2.64) and (2.77) apply with TsT_{s} replaced by the pilot spacing TpT_{p} and N=T~s/TpN=\tilde{T}_{s}/T_{p}. The same trade-off identified for the single-carrier case holds: a smaller pilot spacing permits a faster secondary symbol rate but reduces the SNR available to the secondary detector through the noise bandwidth of the tracking loop. Low-update-rate PLL designs suited to this pilot-driven tracking are treated in [31].

2.3.4 Burst Mode

In burst-mode systems (e.g., IEEE 802.11a/g/n) each transmission is a self-contained burst preceded by a preamble. The preamble—the short and long training sequences (STS/LTS) in 802.11—is used for burst detection, symbol-timing synchronization, channel estimation, and frequency-offset estimation [29]. Two secondary-channel strategies are available, differing in how much of the per-OFDM-symbol structure can be exploited.

Static offset per burst. The simplest strategy applies a single static frequency shift to the entire burst, encoding one secondary symbol per burst. This is discussed and analyzed in more detail in Chapter 4. The receiver recovers the secondary symbol directly from the preamble’s frequency-offset estimate, for example via the Schmidl–Cox estimator applied to the repeated training symbols [29], or via the autocorrelation of the long training sequence. Because the estimate is formed from the (relatively long) preamble, the frequency-estimation error η\eta is small, so the effective secondary SNR is high; the cost is the lowest possible secondary rate of one symbol per burst.

Intra-burst tracking. A higher-rate strategy applies a slowly time-varying phase across the burst and tracks the offset from OFDM symbol to OFDM symbol using the pilot subcarriers embedded in each data symbol [27], [28], [31]. A low-update-rate PLL or per-symbol pilot-based frequency estimator produces one CFO sample per OFDM symbol, recovering the per-symbol observable of (2.85). The secondary rate can then approach the bound (2.86) of one secondary symbol per OFDM symbol, at the cost of the noisier per-symbol (rather than per-preamble) frequency estimates. An intermediate alternative injects an independent static offset on each OFDM symbol and computes an independent frequency-offset estimate per symbol [33].

2.3.5 Rate–Resolution Trade-off

In all multi-carrier modes the secondary symbol rate is bounded above by the CFO-estimation rate—at most once per OFDM symbol (2.86)—even when the underlying protocol could in principle estimate more often. This is more restrictive than the single-carrier case, where the loop produces an estimate every base-protocol symbol. The compensating benefit is that the longer OFDM symbol (and longer secondary symbol) duration permits more accurate frequency estimation: the frequency-estimation variance of a maximum-likelihood estimator scales inversely with the cube of the observation length [34]. The improved frequency resolution allows the secondary channel to use higher-order M~\tilde{M}-ary frequency-shift constellations, recovering some of the throughput that would otherwise be lost to the reduced symbol rate. This is a deliberate exchange of temporal resolution for frequency resolution—the same design philosophy that motivates multi-carrier modulation itself. While most modern multi-carrier receivers do not implement a literal PLL, FLE remains applicable by reading whatever CFO observable the base protocol exposes (a frequency-domain pilot-based estimate, a preamble estimate, or a tracking-loop state), and the high-level detection procedure is unchanged.

3 Simulation

The analysis in the previous chapter provides intuition regarding how the key design parameters, fdTsf_{d}T_{s} and N=T~sTsN=\frac{\tilde{T}_s}{T_s}, affect the performance of both protocols, establishing theoretical boundaries for carrier phase PLL lock. We now determine a more precise set of bounds numerically, integrating real-world factors such as channel impairments, timing synchronization, and protocol overhead. To achieve this, we simulate the complete primary and subprotocol transmit and receive chains, evaluating their performance across a variety of channel models. These simulations are built upon representative single- and multi-carrier underlying protocols. We begin with the foundational AWGN model to sweep across a range of design parameters. Subsequently, we expand our evaluation to standardized ITU [35]a models to incorporate multipath and frequency-selective fading effects.

a The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) channel models are a class of standard mathematical models designed to simulate real-world RF propagation environments, including urban areas, mobility, and crowded buildings.

3.1 System Design

To demonstrate the performance of the single-carrier FLE, we create a GNU Radio implementation, shown in Figure 3.1. The primary signal is QPSK with the square-root raised-cosine (SRRC) pulse shape with unity DC gain and 50% excess bandwidth, and the secondary signal is a binary PAM pulse train using the SRRC pulse shape with 100% excess bandwidth. For computer simulation in the AWGN environment, we add noise with GNU Radio’s channel model block. To evaluate frequency-selective fading, we extend the flowgraph with simulated Tapped Delay Line (TDL) channels configured to ITU specifications. On the primary channel, the receiver recovers symbol timing with the Gardner timing error detector [23] and a Farrow interpolator, and carrier phase with a second-order PLL at a closed-loop equivalent bandwidth BnTs=0.02B_nT_{s}=0.02 cycles/symbol. The secondary detector is the matched filter followed by a second symbol timing synchronizer using the same Gardner timing error detector and Farrow interpolator. We sweep fdTsf_dT_{s} and NN over a range of values and report the results in Section 3.2.

As an example of multi-carrier operation, we use OFDM bursts following the IEEE 802.11 standard. The transmitter injects a frequency offset proportional to the secondary channel PAM symbol into each burst, producing a secondary channel data rate equivalent to one M~\tilde{M}-ary secondary channel symbol per OFDM burst. At the receiver, the Schmidl–Cox algorithm [29] operates on each long training sequence (LTS) to detect the secondary channel symbol.

Section 3.2 describes the experiments with different frequency offsets and different values of M~\tilde{M} under both AWGN and ITU channel models.

3.2 Evaluation

In our evaluation, we seek to answer four main questions:

  1. Does FLE affect the performance of the primary communication link?

  2. Under what conditions can the secondary channel be reliably decoded?

  3. How do the FLE parameters fdTsf_d T_s and NN affect system performance?

  4. How robust is the FLE subprotocol when exposed to real-world multipath delay spread?

Performance is measured using bit error rate (BER) as a function of Eb/N0E_b/N_0 for both the primary and secondary protocols, calculated with the bit energy of the primary protocol.

3.2.1 Single-Carrier Performance

After extensive simulation, we find that although FLE parameters can influence QPSK performance, their impact on the primary protocol remains minimal provided the parameters lie within a defined operating envelope. Figure 3.2(a) shows the BER performance of QPSK under four different FLE configurations, along with a baseline case in which FLE is absent. For reference, the theoretical BER curve under additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) is also included. The observed implementation loss is attributable to the simulation tooling rather than the presence of the subprotocol. Nearly all simulated curves, including the no-FLE case, follow the same trajectory. Only when parameters are pushed to extreme values (e.g., N=16N=16 and fdTs=0.0064f_d T_s=0.0064) does a slight degradation appear; even in this case, the degradation is limited to approximately 1 dB in Eb/N0E_b/N_0. To identify the bounds of this stability envelope, we perform a parameter sweep, shown in Figure 3.2(b). Primary protocol reception remains near perfect below a clear boundary in the NN–fdTsf_d T_s plane, indicating a wide operating region where FLE can coexist with QPSK without significant impact.

In contrast, the effect of FLE parameters on the subprotocol is more prominent. As shown in Figure 3.2(c), both NN and fdTsf_d T_s strongly affect the BER performance of FLE. Increasing these parameters improves subprotocol detectability, but excessive values lead to degradation of the primary protocol, presenting a trade-off to the end user.

Importantly, there exists an overlap region where both the primary protocol and the FLE subprotocol achieve high performance. This is evident from the FLE parameter sweep in Figure 3.2(d). If fdTsf_d T_s is too small, the subprotocol signal is lost in the noise floor; if NN is too low, the PLL cannot reliably lock and track the induced frequency changes. Optimal performance is achieved through a balanced combination of these two parameters. To visualize this stable operating envelope, we overlay the primary and subprotocol BER in Figure 3.3. We present the following as a design rule. We first take the intersection of the primary protocol and subprotocol stability regions and then apply a conservative linear fit to the boundary. This places the operating envelope at:

0.0016≤fdTs≤0.001N+0.0080for N≥120.0016 \le f_d T_s \le 0.001N + 0.0080 \qquad \text{for } N \ge 12(3.1)

For reference, this operating region is now shown against the mathematical bounds computed in the previous chapter as Figure 3.4. The previous analysis only found the bounds on the carrier phase PLL lock. This operating envelope also takes into account the SNR of the subprotocol (i.e., if fdf_d is too low, the subprotocol has very little SNR and is therefore not decodable).

Each of the three edges of (3.1) corresponds to a distinct mechanism identified in Chapter 2, and it is worth taking them in turn, because the envelope is not a single phenomenon but three superimposed ones.

The sloped upper edge is the lock limit. It is linear in NN as (2.80) predicts. Doubling NN halves the modulating frequency and therefore doubles the deviation the loop can follow. Above this edge the base protocol is the layer that fails—the carrier phase PLL slips cycles—and the subprotocol fails with it, since the observable it is read from is the loop that has just lost lock. This represents the principal trade-off with FLE. There is a linear trade-off between subtlety in frequency deviation and speed of the subprotocol.

The horizontal lower edge at fdTs=0.0016f_{d}T_{s}=0.0016 comes from the subprotocol signal-to-noise ratio (2.52) rather than from any lock condition. Below it the deviation is simply too small to lift the subprotocol pulse train clear of the loop-filter noise ν2(kTs)\nu_{2}(kT_{s}), and the subprotocol bit error rate collapses while the base protocol remains entirely untouched. That this edge is flat—independent of NN—is itself predicted by (2.52): the ratio depends on (fdA~)2(f_{d}\tilde{A})^{2}, on I2I_{2}, and on the base protocol’s Eavg/N0E_{avg}/N_{0}, but not on the subprotocol symbol rate. The detection floor is therefore a property of the deviation and the loop, not of how fast the subprotocol is run.

The vertical edge at N=12N=12 is the one the lock limits do not predict, and its absence from (2.80) is not an oversight: those limits bound base-protocol integrity, whereas this edge is a subprotocol reception failure. It is the bandwidth condition on the differentiator approximation (2.41) discussed in Chapter 2. Below N=12N=12 the subprotocol pulse train is no longer narrow compared with the closed-loop bandwidth of the PLL, so the loop stops behaving as a flat differentiator and instead smears the pulse train it is supposed to reproduce. Empirically this edge is found to be abrupt. The subprotocol fails over a single step in NN rather than degrading gradually.

Read together, the three edges say that the usable region is bounded above by the base protocol’s tolerance and below and to the left by the subprotocol’s own detectability. The lock limits alone describe only the first of these, which is why the analytical bounds of Chapter 2 are necessary but not sufficient to place the operating point.

3.2.2 Multi-Carrier Performance

Similar evaluations are performed on the multi-carrier system with several key differences. Both 16-QAM and 64-QAM OFDM symbols are tested to determine whether FLE performance varies with the order of the OFDM constellation and to model both high- and low-data-rate modulations.

Because FLE symbols are applied at the burst level in the multi-carrier system, the parameter NN, defined as the ratio of primary to subprotocol symbols, no longer has a meaningful interpretation. Instead, performance is characterized primarily by the magnitude of the normalized frequency shift, fdTsf_d T_s. As shown in Figure 3.5(a), the presence or absence of FLE has very little effect on the BER trajectory of the OFDM system. While we again see implementation loss from the simulation tooling, this loss is not due to the subprotocol. In the 64-QAM case, we observe a small performance difference with and without the FLE overlay (approximately 0.5% in the worst case); however, this degradation is negligible. We find that any value of fdTsf_d T_s within a stable operating envelope produces a similar effect on the primary protocol. The upper bound of this envelope occurs when the carrier phase synchronization algorithm can no longer reliably correct the induced frequency offset. For the system considered here, which employs the Schmidl–Cox algorithm, this limit is observed at fdTs≈3.2f_d T_s \approx 3.2.

The effect of fdTsf_d T_s on the subprotocol is shown in Figure 3.5(b). These results correspond to 4-ary FLE symbols operating on top of a primary protocol employing a 64-QAM constellation. Once fdTsf_d T_s exceeds the noise floor of the CFO estimator, further increases provide minimal improvement in BER. A lower bound on the stability envelope for the multi-carrier system is observed at fdTs≈0.096f_d T_s \approx 0.096. To maximize subprotocol data rate, higher-order frequency-shift constellations can be employed. At a conservative operating point, where the frequency separation between adjacent subprotocol symbols is fdTs=0.16f_d T_s=0.16, reliable operation is achieved with modulation orders up to 32-ary PAM.

3.3 Complex Environments

The preceding evaluation establishes the operating envelope of FLE under idealized AWGN conditions, answering Questions 1–3. We now turn to Question 4: how robust is the subprotocol under realistic multipath propagation? To this end, we subject the same single- and multi-carrier systems to standardized ITU channel models, specifically the Extended Pedestrian A (EPA) and Extended Vehicular A (EVA) delay profiles [35]. EPA represents a mild pedestrian scenario with seven taps spanning 410 ns of delay spread, while EVA models a more severe vehicular environment with nine taps and a maximum excess delay of 2.51 μ\mus. Both profiles are implemented as TDL channels with randomized tap phases, producing independent static fading snapshots for each trial. All sweeps use an SNR of Eb/N0=18E_b/N_0 = 18 dB, identical to the AWGN baseline.

Because fading channels introduce stochastic variation—a single channel realization may place a deep spectral null near the carrier frequency, preventing lock, while an adjacent realization may produce a benign response—we employ a Monte Carlo approach with 10 independent trials per (N,fdTs)(N, f_d T_s) cell for the fading channels (EPA and EVA), each with a different initial phase. We compare these against the deterministic AWGN baseline sweep of Section 3.2.1. This design allows us to report the mean BER at each operating point from which we calculate the probability of achieving PLL lock (which we define as BER ≤10−3\leq 10^{-3}). This provides a more complete characterization of the fading operating envelope than any single realization can offer.

3.3.1 Channel Effect on Subprotocol

For the single-carrier system, the introduction of multipath fading significantly stresses the synchronization loops. The carrier phase PLL must now track not only thermal noise and FLE frequency deviations, but also the phase rotations introduced by the multipath taps. We find the latter noise source to be the dominating factor as shown below. Figure 3.6 presents the parameter-space heatmaps under all three channel conditions, where each cell now represents the mean BER averaged over 10 independent channel realizations for the multipath channels.

Under AWGN, the single-trial sweep produces a smooth, repeatable contour, with no mixed outcomes due to the deterministic channel. Under EPA, the envelope contracts sharply: only 0.5% of cells achieved lock on all 10 trials, while 54.9% exhibited mixed outcomes—sometimes locking, sometimes failing, depending entirely on the particular channel draw. This stochasticity is evident in the speckled EPA panels of Figure 3.6, where adjacent cells differ sharply, in contrast to the smooth contour of the deterministic AWGN sweep. Under EVA, the envelope collapses entirely: no cells achieved lock on all trials, and only 0.9% ever locked at all. The mean FLE BER reached 0.458, approaching the random-guessing floor. A Kruskal–Wallis test confirmed the channel as the dominant factor in FLE decodability (H=12,513H = 12{,}513, p<10−16p < 10^{-16}). These results are summarized in Table 3.1.

Table 3.1 Single-Carrier FLE Performance (N≥12N \geq 12, fd>0f_d > 0)
MetricAWGNEPAEVA
Mean FLE BER0.0460.1850.458
Overall lock rate78.3%22.2%0.1%
Cells that always lock78.3%0.5%0.0%
Cells with mixed outcomes0.0%54.9%0.9%
Mean QPSK BER0.0220.0840.360

The multi-carrier system tells a dramatically different story. The cyclic prefix absorbs any inter-symbol interference introduced by the multipath environment. This, coupled with per-subcarrier equalization, recovers the QAM payloads much more accurately than the single-carrier equivalent. Furthermore, because the mechanism used for our multi-carrier simulation relies on a per-packet frequency offset, the CFO estimation is highly robust, deriving from the STS and LTS of the 802.11 preamble. Unsurprisingly, and as shown in Figure 3.7, FLE achieves perfect decoding (BER =0.0= 0.0) across all tested fdf_d values under both EPA and EVA. The multipath channel that destroys single-carrier FLE has virtually no effect on the multi-carrier variant.

3.3.2 Effect of the Subprotocol on the Primary Protocol

Having established that the channel degrades single-carrier FLE while leaving multi-carrier FLE unaffected, we now ask whether the presence of FLE worsens the primary protocol under these harsher conditions. This is the central question for system design: even if the subprotocol itself fails, it must not take the primary link down with it. The dataset provides 23,520 total observations, yielding substantial statistical power to detect even small interaction effects. As we show below, the answer has two layers: FLE is transparent to the primary protocol on average, yet its parameters and the channel genuinely interact in shaping how the carrier phase PLL acquires lock.

Figure 3.8 compares QPSK BER distributions with FLE off (fd=0f_d = 0) versus FLE active (fd>0f_d > 0) across all three channels. The overlap of the distributions is striking. We conduct a Type II two-way ANOVA on QPSK BER, treating FLE state (active vs. off) and channel as factors and identify the channel model as the sole significant factor (F=11,096F = 11{,}096, η2=0.486\eta^2 = 0.486, p<10−16p < 10^{-16}). Neither the FLE main effect (p=0.813p = 0.813) nor the FLE ×\times channel interaction (p=0.632p = 0.632) reaches significance. On average, the mere presence of the subprotocol neither degrades the primary protocol nor amplifies the channel’s degradation; FLE is transparent to the primary link in the aggregate, as the overlap of the FLE-off and FLE-active distributions in Figure 3.8 makes plain.

While the aggregate statistics show no interaction between FLE and the channel on primary link performance, a closer look reveals a real physical interaction between the FLE parameters and the channel that dictates exactly where the carrier phase PLL acquires lock. Because the temporal span of the subprotocol symbols can approach the characteristic delays of the channel taps, delayed copies of the signal arrive and overlap across the FLE symbol boundaries. This temporal smearing effectively low-pass filters or “rounds out” the abrupt, extreme phase transitions that occur at the edges of the frequency-shifted symbols.

This rounding effect explains the distinct presence of “rescue cells” in the parameter space. Under AWGN, 260 active configurations drove QPSK out of lock—all concentrated at high frequency deviations (fdTs≥0.024f_d T_s \geq 0.024), where clean, sharp phase transitions consistently provoke cycle slips. Yet under the EPA channel, every one of these configurations recovered lock in at least one realization, and 220 locked in the majority of realizations. Because the multipath taps smooth the transition boundaries, they significantly reduce the peak instantaneous phase derivatives presented to the loop filter. The channel effectively rescues the primary link from configurations that would predictably force a cycle slip in a clean environment.

This rescue is uniquely an EPA phenomenon: under EVA, the delay spread is so severe that the PLL is saturated by the channel itself. Only 60 of the 260 cells ever recovered, and then only sporadically. Once fading dominates, the multipath-induced phase and amplitude fluctuations dwarf the FLE deviations entirely, rendering the subprotocol’s perturbation undetectable.

It is worth noting that for the single-carrier system, the question of whether the primary protocol is disproportionately affected by the subprotocol in these complex environments is largely moot. In practice, a bare-bones single-carrier protocol would not be deployed in such harsh multipath conditions, as the standard PLL already experiences severe difficulty acquiring and maintaining lock.

For the multi-carrier system, the previous conclusions hold. The OFDM payload experiences the expected modulation-order-dependent degradation—64-QAM BER rises from 6.3×10−56.3 \times 10^{-5} under EPA to 4.1×10−34.1 \times 10^{-3} under EVA—but this degradation shows no correlation with fdf_d (Spearman ρ=0.052\rho = 0.052, p=0.903p = 0.903 for EPA; ρ=0.000\rho = 0.000, p=1.000p = 1.000 for EVA). The OFDM payload remains entirely unaffected by the subprotocol’s presence. One could imagine a “straw that broke the camel’s back” scenario in which the multi-carrier link is already teetering on the edge of failure, and the small, added frequency offset of the subprotocol finally breaks it. However, encountering an environment balanced so precisely on this precipice is exceptionally rare. Modern OFDM systems typically employ robust rate adaptation, dynamically downshifting to a lower-order modulation scheme well before a fractional frequency offset becomes the dominant cause of failure. Furthermore, the residual phase errors introduced by FLE are easily absorbed by the continuous phase tracking of the pilot subcarriers, meaning that if the link drops, it is almost certainly due to deep multipath fading rather than the subprotocol. Should such a highly specific marginal condition arise, higher-layer feedback could simply instruct the transmitter to temporarily cease subprotocol transmissions.

3.3.3 Summary

The Monte Carlo evaluation across complex channel models supports a three-part conclusion. First, the single-carrier FLE subprotocol is sensitive to the propagation environment: the lock envelope contracts from a 78.3% rate under AWGN to 22.2% under EPA—with 54.9% of EPA cells exhibiting stochastic, realization-dependent locking—and collapses to 0.1% under EVA. The multi-carrier variant, by contrast, is immune; it leverages the robust CFO estimation to achieve perfect FLE decoding even under the most severe delay profile. Second, the presence of FLE does not degrade the primary protocol on average. For the single-carrier system, the FLE-on and FLE-off QPSK distributions remain statistically indistinguishable under fading. For the multi-carrier system, the OFDM payload is entirely unaffected by the subprotocol, with marginal failure scenarios being exceedingly rare and easily mitigated. Third, there exists a real physical interaction between the frequency shift parameters and the channel that dictates exactly where the carrier phase PLL acquires lock. Under AWGN, sharp, extreme phase transitions at high frequency deviations reliably provoke cycle slips; however, the temporal smearing of the EPA delay spread smooths these transition boundaries, rescuing the primary link in precisely the configurations where a clean channel fails. The channel and the subprotocol thus interact in shaping the parameter space of the primary lock, but this interaction redistributes rather than amplifies error, leaving FLE transparent to the primary protocol in the aggregate.

4 Implementation

Having established the mathematical foundation of FLE in Chapter 2 and validated it through simulation in Chapter 3, we now realize the system over the air. We begin with SDR experiments that confirm FLE works as predicted, but SDRs are laboratory instruments, not consumer devices. For potential applications, an implementation on 802.11 Wi-Fi commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware is extremely desirable. This chapter introduces the adaptation of FLE for COTS hardware and addresses the unique chain of challenges that such an implementation encounters. The end result is a fully functional FLE transmitter and receiver that works completely in software on COTS devices. The evaluation of this complete system under real-world conditions is presented in Chapter 5 alongside two applications.

4.1 SDR Implementation

Using the same GRC environment outlined in Section 3.1, we transmit our FLE overlay over the air in real-time on top of both single-carrier and multi-carrier modulations, as shown in Figure 4.1. We use two USRP B210 SDRs as the transmitter and receiver of the primary protocol, labeled Primary TX and Primary RX in the figure. The transmitter is configured to concurrently transmit FLE data. We use the ADALM-Pluto SDR as a secondary RX, which passively monitors the transmission and extracts only the FLE information embedded as frequency offsets. Using the relatively inexpensive Pluto SDR shows the low barrier to entry for our protocol and the universality of this design across different hardware capabilities. For our over-the-air experiments, we transmit over the unlicensed 915 MHz band.

4.1.1 Over-the-Air Tests

For the over-the-air experiments, we select robust operating parameters from the simulation results for both the single-carrier and multi-carrier systems. These experiments serve as a preliminary feasibility study, not a full validation, since the desired end result is on different hardware. The specific parameters used are as follows:

  • Single-Carrier: Primary protocol = QPSK, N=32N = 32, fdTs=0.0096f_d T_s = 0.0096

  • Multi-Carrier: Primary protocol = 16-QAM, subprotocol = 4-ary PAM, fdTs=0.16f_d T_s = 0.16

We conducted experiments at transmitter–receiver separations of 1 m and 20 m. At the shorter distance, both the primary and secondary protocols achieved near-perfect reception in the single-carrier and multi-carrier configurations, as expected. At the increased separation, the single-carrier system continued to exhibit excellent performance, with both the primary protocol and the subprotocol achieving measured BERs on the order of 10−610^{-6}. In the multi-carrier system, the primary protocol experienced a higher BER due to the use of a higher-order constellation.

Although the observed BERs were ultimately determined by the SNR conditions of the two scenarios, the key result is that the primary protocol and the subprotocol exhibited similar error-rate trends and operational ranges. This is precisely the behavior predicted by (2.52): the signal-to-noise ratio at the subprotocol detector is directly proportional to the Eavg/N0E_{avg}/N_{0} of the base protocol, so the two channels track one another as the link budget changes rather than failing at independent thresholds. The subprotocol has no noise budget of its own; it borrows the base protocol’s, and the over-the-air measurements show it inheriting the base protocol’s operating range as a consequence. These experiments demonstrate that the secondary signaling layer can closely track the reliability of the underlying communication system while remaining effectively transparent to the primary protocol. In tested configurations, the subprotocol achieved data rates exceeding 900 kbps, with performance ultimately limited by the computational capability of the laptops running GNU Radio Companion rather than by the FLE mechanism itself.

4.2 COTS Hardware

The SDR experiments confirm that FLE works over the air, but SDRs offer complete control over the transmit chain—a luxury that consumer hardware does not provide. The next step is to demonstrate FLE on commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) devices where the radio is managed by a closed-source firmware stack. We use two ESP32-C5 microcontrollers as the transmitter and receiver, and show that controlled frequency impairments can be introduced and detected exclusively via software, requiring no hardware modifications.a As we will see, solving the physical-layer access problem is only the first step: the full IEEE 802.11ax MAC layer introduces a cascade of timing and channel challenges that do not exist on an SDR.

a Although several of the employed techniques are specific to the ESP32-C5 silicon, the fundamental concepts can be generalized to other microcontroller architectures. Notably, we have successfully created a transmitter on the ESP32-S3 architecture.

4.2.1 FLE COTS Physical Layer

Every modern Wi-Fi receiver maintains a real-time estimate of the carrier-frequency offset (CFO) between itself and the incoming transmitter to prevent inter-carrier interference caused by local oscillator mismatch. This offset arises from crystal tolerances and Doppler effects and is normally corrected transparently by the receiver’s automatic frequency correction (AFC) loop. In a modern Wi-Fi stack, this is done using the short training sequence (STS) and long training sequence (LTS) at the beginning of an IEEE 802.11 burst.

The STS consists of 10 identical repetitions. These repetitions allow the receiver to perform a rapid, coarse CFO estimation without phase ambiguity. Let y[n]y[n] denote the received discrete-time baseband signal. By calculating the autocorrelation between adjacent STS repetitions separated by NSTSN_{\text{STS}} samples, the receiver estimates the coarse frequency offset [29]:

Δfcoarse=12πNSTSTsamp∠(∑n=0NSTS−1y*[n]y[n+NSTS])\Delta f_{\text{coarse}} = \frac{1}{2 \pi N_{\text{STS}} T_{\text{samp}}} \angle \left( \sum_{n=0}^{N_{\text{STS}}-1} y^*[n] y[n+N_{\text{STS}}] \right)(4.1)

where TsampT_{\text{samp}} is the sampling period. Once this coarse offset is compensated for in the time domain, the receiver uses the LTS for fine CFO estimation.

The LTS consists of a long guard interval followed by two identical, full-length OFDM symbols. Because these two symbols are transmitted consecutively and separated by NLTSN_{\text{LTS}} samples (e.g., NLTS=64N_{\text{LTS}} = 64 for a standard 20 MHz channel), any remaining phase drift between the first and second symbol is strictly due to the residual frequency offset. The receiver computes the autocorrelation RR between the corresponding samples of the two LTS symbols:

R=∑n=0NLTS−1y*[n]y[n+NLTS]R = \sum_{n=0}^{N_{\text{LTS}}-1} y^*[n] y[n+N_{\text{LTS}}](4.2)

The phase of this autocorrelation represents the total phase rotation Δθ=∠R\Delta \theta = \angle R over the duration of one LTS sequence. The fine CFO, Δffine\Delta f_{\text{fine}}, is mathematically derived as [36]:

Δffine=Δθ2πNLTSTsamp\Delta f_{\text{fine}} = \frac{\Delta \theta}{2 \pi N_{\text{LTS}} T_{\text{samp}}}(4.3)

Both estimators are instances of the maximum-likelihood autocorrelation-based frequency estimator. The estimation variance as a function of SNR follows from the statistics of the autocorrelation phase [36]:

σn2=1(2π)2Nlag2Tsamp2L⋅SNR(1+12SNR)\sigma_n^2 = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^2 N_{\text{lag}}^2 T_{\text{samp}}^2 \, L \cdot \text{SNR}} \left(1 + \frac{1}{2\,\text{SNR}}\right)(4.4)

where NlagN_{\text{lag}} is the correlation lag in samples (NSTSN_{\text{STS}} or NLTSN_{\text{LTS}}) and LL is the number of sample pairs in the summation. At moderate-to-high SNR the second term vanishes and the variance decreases inversely with SNR, so the CFO estimate exploited by FLE grows more precise as link quality improves—the same relationship derived for the phase estimate in (2.52), here reduced further by the robust LTS/STS training sequence.

The key detail is that a method of very precise frequency estimation and correction is innate to the structure of the Wi-Fi stack. Just as with any wireless protocol, we can leverage this process to enable a subprotocol channel.

4.2.2 Hardware Register Manipulation

By default, the ESP32 family of microcontrollers does not expose RF statistics regarding the CFO to the application layer. These calculations are executed directly within the silicon, typically requiring no software interface. However, we discovered that during the AFC process, the hardware records the CFO of each incoming packet into a dedicated hardware register. By accessing this register at the correct stage of the reception pipeline, we can accurately detect the FLE signal.

Furthermore, the ESP32 silicon contains a fractional-NN divider responsible for tuning the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz oscillators. While this divider is normally managed by the closed-source Wi-Fi stack binary via a control register, we were able to experimentally map its behavior. By writing a wide range of values to this register and measuring the induced CFO using an SDR, we characterized the exact frequency offsets produced. These induced offsets are highly reliable and repeatable. Figure 4.2 shows the successful mapping to produce a wide range of desired frequency offsets as measured by a highly reliable USRP X410 SDR.b By leveraging these two undocumented registers, we successfully implemented both an FLE transmitter and receiver entirely in software.

b These frequency offsets are highly accurate and reproducible, but still contain an uncontrollable static frequency offset from oscillator mismatch.

The transmitter tunes the microcontroller’s oscillator across a wide range of fdf_d values to transmit symbols from 𝒜~\mathcal{\tilde{A}}, its alphabet of M~\tilde{M}-ary symbols, with high precision. Upon packet detection, the receiver simply reads the designated hardware register to extract its CFO estimate.

4.2.3 The Observation Channel

With both registers in hand, the subprotocol has a viable COTS transmitter and a receiver. We now turn to describing the channel it must use, which is unusual in several respects. Every received Wi-Fi packet leaves behind exactly one CFO reading, which consists of the FLE symbol, noise, and thermal and electrical effects from the two oscillators. The estimation noise of (4.4) is only one component of the offset the receiver actually observes. Over a run of received packets indexed by ii, the measured offset Δfi^\widehat{\Delta f_i} decomposes into a static term, two slowly-varying terms, and the estimation noise:

Δfi^=Δf0⏟static+d(ti)⏟thermal drift+η(ti)⏟random wander+ni⏟estimation noise\widehat{\Delta f_i} \;=\; \underbrace{\Delta f_0}_{\text{static}} \;+\; \underbrace{d(t_i)}_{\text{thermal drift}} \;+\; \underbrace{\eta(t_i)}_{\text{random wander}} \;+\; \underbrace{n_i}_{\text{estimation noise}}(4.5)

The static offset Δf0\Delta f_0 is a fixed bias from crystal tolerance—measured between roughly 3,0003{,}000 and 6,0006{,}000 Hz across our devices—that is constant over a session. The thermal drift d(ti)d(t_i) is a slow, near-deterministic trend as the oscillator warms, on the order of tens of hertz per second (about 23 Hz/s on average, and as steep as 135 Hz/s within a single frame in our measurements), evolving over minutes. The random wander η(ti)\eta(t_i) is a zero-mean, temporally correlated meander from oscillator phase and flicker noise, with a standard deviation of roughly 150–300 Hz and a correlation time of one to two seconds. Only the final term nin_i is an independent per-packet error, with the variance of (4.4) (a standard deviation near 500 Hz on a typical Wi-Fi link). This separation is what makes the channel tractable: the first three terms vary slowly and together form a wandering baseline that the receiver can track and subtract, while the last is a per-packet random error. The receiver’s treatment of each term is detailed in Chapter 5.

The other and more dominant characteristic of the FLE-on-COTS Wi-Fi channel is the symbol rate. Equation (2.86) dictates that the FLE symbol rate in a multi-carrier system is bounded by a minimum requirement of N=1N=1 primary packet per FLE symbol. A COTS Wi-Fi implementation, however, cannot directly map FLE symbols to Wi-Fi packets because Wi-Fi traffic is inherently bursty. Although the Wi-Fi symbol time TsymT_{\text{sym}} is fixed, the time between packets is not. Moreover, the MAC layer introduces additional uncertainty through channel sensing, Request-to-Send (RTS) and Clear-to-Send (CTS) exchanges, retransmissions, packet aggregation, and management frames associated with authentication, handshaking, and acknowledgments. Many of these events occur without the knowledge or control of higher-layer applications, making packet dispatch times impossible to predict. Consequently, neither a fixed FLE symbol rate based solely on the packet rate λ\lambda nor a symbol rate that varies directly with λ\lambda is practical.

Instead, the subprotocol symbol time T~s\tilde{T}_s must be chosen independently of λ\lambda, while still being informed by the traffic rate and other transmission characteristics. The subprotocol therefore runs on its own clock, selecting T~s\tilde{T}_s in advance and holding it for the duration of a frame. Primary Wi-Fi packets then fall wherever they occur within these symbol windows, and each FLE symbol is decoded from whatever CFO observations happen to be available during its window. The transmitter must therefore select T~s\tilde{T}_s to maximize the probability of successful symbol recovery. This predictable symbol clock produces a channel unlike a conventional wireless channel. Because a primary Wi-Fi packet is not guaranteed to occur in every symbol window, some windows contain no CFO observation at all.

In summary, the channel experiences two independent classes of impairments:

  1. Analog impairments. Additive white Gaussian noise, multipath fading, crystal oscillator drift, and quantization noise in the CFO estimator produce random bit errors in the recovered symbols. These are the same impairments analyzed in Chapter 2 and are governed by the receiver signal-to-noise ratio, as quantified by (4.4).

  2. PHY and MAC layer erasures. Contention backoffs, idle periods, and traffic gaps can leave a symbol window with no primary transmission from which to obtain a CFO observation. Because the transmitter and receiver share the FLE symbol clock, the location of every expected symbol is known. If no valid CFO sample is observed within a window, the receiver therefore marks that symbol as an erasure—an unknown value at a known index—rather than as an erroneous bit.

Critically, the second and dominant impairment makes the implementation an erasure-dominant channel rather than a deletion channel. With erasures, the position of every missing symbol remains known. This positional information allows an appropriate error-correcting code to recover from erasures more efficiently than from unknown-position deletions.

4.2.4 Traffic Characterization

To inform the selection of T~s\tilde{T}_s and any subsequent erasure-tolerant coding, we first examine the behavior of typical Wi-Fi device traffic. To that end, we captured real IEEE 802.11 traffic from commodity access points and client devices across six representative usage scenarios: a Zoom video call, a large file transfer, Instagram browsing, web surfing, YouTube streaming, and an access point serving multiple clients simultaneously. For these scenarios, we examine only the packets transmitted, and not received, by each device.c

c In terms of volume of data, the uplink of video streaming, web surfing, and social media usage is not very large. FLE, however, needs a large number of packets, not data. In light of this, we examine whether ACKs and the small amount of uplink in these usual activities provide enough of a carrier signal.

Figure 4.3 presents the packet rate over time for each scenario, with individual packet arrivals shown as tick marks along the time axis. The contrast is immediate: Zoom produces a nearly continuous stream of codec frames with only mild fluctuations around the mean, while YouTube’s sparse bursts are separated by multi-second silences due to its buffering behavior. The large file transfer exhibits the highest peak rates, with TCP-driven bursts exceeding 1000 packets/s before dropping to zero during congestion-window resets. The remaining scenarios fall between these extremes, but none resemble a constant-rate source.

While the time-domain view illustrates the problem qualitatively, we ask a more precise question for the FLE-on-COTS implementation: for a given symbol period T~s\tilde{T}_s, what fraction of symbol windows will contain zero primary packets and therefore produce an erasure? Figure 4.4 plots this erasure probability as a function of T~s\tilde{T}_s for each scenario. At a symbol period of 50 ms, Zoom drops below 4% erasure probability, but YouTube still exceeds 70%. Even at T~s=200\tilde{T}_s = 200 ms—the slowest MCS in our system—YouTube erases half of all symbol slots. The large file transfer, despite averaging 671 packets/s, still erases a quarter of its slots at 25 ms, because its traffic arrives in intense bursts separated by quiet intervals rather than as a steady stream. These curves directly inform subprotocol parameter selection. A traffic pattern with a steep erasure curve can sustain a shorter symbol period and therefore a higher data rate, while a pattern with a shallow curve requires a longer period and heavier error-correction overhead.

Channel Characterization Plane

The erasure curve is the quantity the subprotocol must survive, but it is not something the transmitter can look up. It is a whole curve, measured against symbol periods the transmitter has not chosen yet. What the transmitter needs is a small, fixed set of statistics from which those curves can be predicted. After examining over 90 statistics, we found that two are sufficient to explain 98% of the subprotocol transmission success rate.

The first is the mean rate λ^\hat{\lambda}, in packets per second. While the subprotocol cannot know the future of what the main protocol will transmit, this rate serves as a predictor of how many observations a symbol of a given duration can expect, N^=λ^T~s\hat{N} = \hat{\lambda}\tilde{T}_s. The second must describe the shape of the arrival process: how the same average rate is distributed in time. Two sources at identical λ^\hat{\lambda} can differ entirely in how their idle time is packaged, and a block code cares a great deal about the difference—twenty percent of slots erased uniformly is a far easier load than the same twenty percent arriving in contiguous runs.

This quantity is the index of dispersion for counts (IDC), the variance-to-mean ratio of the arrival count in a window. The IDC must be defined carefully, because a naive definition over a window of fixed duration inherits several defects. First, Wi-Fi traffic is approximately scale-free—the gap distribution follows a power law over the timescales of interest [37]—so the IDC measured over a window of duration TT climbs monotonically with TT and never plateaus. Across our captures it rises by nearly two orders of magnitude between window sizes of 25 ms and 30 s. Second, and more damaging for our purposes, a wall-clock window holds a number of packets proportional to the rate, so a fixed-duration IDC is not comparable between two sources of different λ^\hat{\lambda}.

Both defects disappear if the window is measured in packets rather than in seconds. We therefore define the dispersion of a carrier as the index of dispersion for counts over a window sized to hold ten arrivals on average, W=10/λ^W = 10/\hat{\lambda}:

I^10=Var(C(W))E[C(W)],W=10λ^\hat{I}_{10} = \frac{\operatorname{Var}\bigl(C(W)\bigr)}{E\bigl[C(W)\bigr]}, \qquad W = \frac{10}{\hat{\lambda}}(4.6)

where C(W)C(W) is the number of packets observed in a window of duration WW. Because the window scales with the rate, I^10\hat{I}_{10} is invariant to λ^\hat{\lambda} at fixed dimensionless arrival shape. A perfectly regular source has I^10=0\hat{I}_{10} = 0, and values grow with clustering. I^10\hat{I}_{10} reveals whether those erasures will arrive as isolated events or as contiguous bursts.

Taken together, (λ^,I^10)(\hat{\lambda}, \hat{I}_{10}) span a plane on which any prospective carrier can be placed with two measurements. Figure 4.5 locates the six captured scenarios on it, along with two engineered reference carriers that bracket what a COTS deployment can arrange deliberately rather than merely observe: a saturating constant stream at one packet every 10 ms, and an access point emitting nothing but beacons at the standard 102.4 ms interval. Both are exactly periodic, so both sit at I^10=0\hat{I}_{10} = 0, though in practical over-the-air scenarios with channel sensing and backoffs, these values are non-zero though very small.

4.2.5 Transmit Rate Adaptation

To obtain both of these metrics on the ESP32, we leverage a hardware callback provided by the ESP32 SDK. The tx_done flag is asserted when the lower MAC finishes processing a transmit descriptor—an event that typically, but not necessarily, corresponds to a completed RF emission. Under queue saturation, the MAC may silently discard frames while still reporting success, though in practice these events are found to be rare.

The transmitter timestamps every tx_done callback during an observation window and reduces that timestamp series to exactly the two coordinates of Section 4.2.4: the mean rate λ^\hat{\lambda} and the dispersion I^10\hat{I}_{10} of (4.6). Both are cheap—a counter and a single pass of variance accumulation over windows sized from the running rate estimate—and neither requires storing the timestamps themselves. The optimal FLE symbol period T~s\tilde{T}_s is then applied based on these statistics.

Figure 4.6 shows the first usage of this subprotocol symbol clock at T~s=200ms\tilde{T}_s=200~\text{ms}, independent of the packet rate, once again measured with a USRP X410 SDR.

The decoupling of the packet rate λ\lambda and T~s\tilde{T}_s yields a powerful result. The FLE-on-COTS application does not need to know anything about the primary protocol’s traffic, because FLE-on-COTS can characterize it and dynamically adjust its own rate to match.

4.3 Coding for the Erasure Channel

Under the assumption of an erasure-prone channel, we employ a coding scheme tailored to such impairments, specifically Reed–Solomon (RS) codes over GF(28)\text{GF}(2^8). These are provably optimal for this purpose.

The Singleton bound [38] establishes a fundamental limit on the minimum distance of any [n,k][n, k] block code over a finite field of order qq:

dmin≤n−k+1d_{\min} \leq n - k + 1(4.7)

A code that achieves this bound with equality is termed a maximum distance separable (MDS) code. Reed–Solomon codes are MDS [39]: for an RS(n,k)(n, k) code with P=n−kP = n - k parity symbols,

dmin=P+1d_{\min} = P + 1(4.8)

On a pure erasure channel, where the decoder knows the locations of all corrupted symbols, each erasure can be corrected with a single parity symbol. An RS(n,k)(n, k) code therefore corrects up to PP erasures:

e≤P=n−ke \leq P = n - k(4.9)

Because of the Singleton bound (4.7), no code with PP parity symbols can correct more than PP erasures. RS codes are therefore optimal for erasure correction: they extract the maximum possible correction from every parity symbol.

On our specific channel, where both random bit errors (EE) and positional erasures (ee) coexist, the RS decoder’s correction capacity follows the well-known mixed bound [40]:

2E+e≤P2E + e \leq P(4.10)

Each random error consumes two parity symbols—one to locate it, one to correct it—while each erasure consumes only one, since its location is already known. The decoder dynamically shares the parity budget PP across both impairment types, dedicating more capacity to erasures when the traffic pattern is bursty and more to random errors when the analog channel is noisy. Our implementation uses the Berlekamp–Massey algorithm [41] for key-equation solving and Forney’s algorithm [42] for error-value computation.

4.3.1 Block Interleaving

Reed–Solomon codes extract the maximum correction from every parity symbol—but this optimality is per-codeword. In practice, we found that RS coding alone is insufficient when MAC-layer erasures arrive in contiguous bursts. A single traffic gap spanning BB consecutive symbol slots would erase BB consecutive bytes in a serial codeword; if B>PB > P, the codeword is unrecoverable regardless of the code’s optimality. To distribute burst erasures across multiple independent codewords, we employ a two-dimensional block interleaving scheme.

The encoded data is arranged as a D×nD \times n matrix where each of the DD rows is an independent RS(n,k)(n, k) codeword. The matrix is transmitted column-major: consecutive bytes on the air correspond to consecutive rows within the same column. A contiguous burst of BB erased bytes therefore scatters across min(B,D)\min(B, D) distinct rows, with each row accumulating at most ⌈B/D⌉\lceil B / D \rceil erasures. The worst-case correctable burst length is:

Bmax=D⋅ProwB_{\max} = D \cdot P_{\text{row}}(4.11)

where ProwP_{\text{row}} is the per-row parity budget. This interleaving transforms a single catastrophic burst into a manageable per-row erasure load, enabling the system to survive traffic gaps far longer than any individual codeword could tolerate. The specific matrix geometry and its interaction with the packet architecture are detailed in Chapter 5.

The combination of RS coding and block interleaving provides a strong defense: the code is optimal for the erasure channel by the Singleton bound, and the interleaver ensures that the bursty erasure patterns characteristic of Wi-Fi traffic are presented to each codeword in a form the code can correct.

4.4 Summary

This chapter shows that FLE operates over the air in both single- and multi-carrier systems, from SDRs to COTS IEEE 802.11ax hardware. On the ESP32-C5, closed-source firmware requires reverse-engineering two undocumented registers for writing and reading the carrier offset. Because these offsets arrive independently of the subprotocol, FLE symbols cannot map directly to Wi-Fi packets. Instead, we decouple the FLE symbol clock from the base protocol. This makes erasures a function of the underlying traffic, which we characterize using two measurable parameters: rate and dispersion, obtained from the tx_done callback. These parameters determine the required Reed–Solomon coding and block interleaving to correct Wi-Fi’s bursty erasures. Together, physical-layer access, an independent symbol clock, traffic-aware rate adaptation, erasure coding, and interleaving enable FLE deployment on COTS hardware. Chapter 5 evaluates these techniques under real-world traffic and presents two FLE applications.

5 Applications

Chapter 4 established the COTS physical-layer adaptation, characterized the unusual channel it produces, identified the traffic observables that inform rate selection, and derived the coding needed to survive the resulting erasures. This chapter builds two applications of FLE on that substrate. Because the channel allows for a much lower data rate than the underlying traffic—delivered whenever the primary link happens to transmit—we begin by stating what a channel of that shape is for, so that the design decisions which follow can be read against the problems they are meant to serve. We then present UnderTone, which turns FLE into a complete general-purpose link on the ESP32-C5, and evaluate its performance over the air. Finally we present SpectralSeal, which applies FLE on the same COTS substrate to physical-layer access-point authentication, serving the third of the use cases named at the outset.

5.1 Motivating Use Cases

The channel that Chapter 4 produces has comparatively low throughput, on the order of tens to hundreds of bits per second. However, it costs no spectrum of its own, requires no modification to the IEEE 802.11 standard, and needs no cooperation from the network that either endpoint is attached to, because it is carried on traffic that was going to be sent regardless and is read from a quantity that every receiver already estimates.

That combination is a poor fit for moving data, and this work does not claim otherwise. It is a good fit for three use cases in which the obstacle has never been capacity. We state them ahead of the construction, because they are what the design choices in the remainder of the chapter are answerable to: a channel of this shape is worth engineering only if the thing one wants to send is small, tolerant of latency, and difficult to send any other way.

5.1.1 Spectrum Coordination

Devices that share a band frequently cannot communicate with one another. Two networks operating on the same channel, or a Wi-Fi network and an unrelated emitter nearby, have no common protocol through which to negotiate coexistence; carrier sensing arbitrates individual transmissions but cannot express intent. Proposals to do better generally assume a control channel, but a control channel is costly precisely because it requires additional spectrum, a standard, or both.

FLE provides such a channel without either. It rides on a carrier a device already emits, requiring no additional airtime, and is extracted from a quantity that receivers already estimate. The peer therefore needs no new protocol layer—only the ability to observe the signal. More importantly, FLE does not require network membership. An 802.11 frame is broadcast at the physical layer, while network membership is a MAC-layer abstraction that does not affect RF reception. A receiver can therefore extract an FLE stream from frames not addressed to it, from a different network, or while associated with no network at all. Section 5.2.5 enumerates the configurations this permits; for spectrum coordination, the important case is precisely the relationship that two uncoordinated networks already have with one another. The reception requirement reduces to sharing an RF channel, which devices contending for that spectrum necessarily do.

The available rates are sufficient for this role. A coordination message might request a channel, report utilization, request deferral, or convey an identifier—tens of bits rather than kilobytes. Section 5.2.3 finds several bits per second available across the region of the carrier plane in Chapter 4 where measured traffic resides, increasing to tens of bits per second when the carrier is deliberately generated. Latency, rather than throughput, is therefore the binding constraint: every frame begins with a fixed, deliberately slow header, making the shortest useful exchange several seconds long. This is appropriate for spectrum etiquette negotiated over minutes, but not for per-frame scheduling. The data rate should nevertheless increase in precisely the scenarios where coordination is most valuable. The traffic best suited to carrying a coordination message is heavy traffic, and heavy traffic is also what creates the contention that motivates coordination in the first place.

5.1.2 Steganography

FLE is not necessarily a covert channel in the strict sense of being statistically indistinguishable from ordinary wireless behavior. Rather, it places information in a measurement that conventional wireless monitoring does not typically expose, while simultaneously obscuring the relationship between transmitter and receiver. FLE adds no frames, changes no packet fields, and requires no additional airtime. Instead, it modulates carrier frequency within transmissions that already exist, using a quantity that conventional receivers estimate as part of synchronization and then discard. A conventional wireless monitor therefore observes the same packets, addresses, and timing as it would without FLE, but does not normally retain the per-frame frequency estimates needed to recover the embedded information.

The ambiguity is particularly useful because FLE is carried at the physical layer rather than being tied to a particular packet exchange. A receiver can observe the modulation without being associated with the transmitting network or being the intended recipient of the underlying frames. Consequently, observing an FLE stream does not by itself reveal which devices are communicating through it: the carrier may be received by any device within range, while the underlying 802.11 traffic may be addressed to an entirely different station. FLE therefore separates the presence of the embedded information from the identities and associations exposed by conventional network-layer monitoring.

5.1.3 Wireless Security

The third use case is wireless authentication. A client selecting an access point may encounter multiple transmitters advertising the same network identity, including a legitimate access point and a rogue transmitter impersonating it. Before association, however, the client has no established relationship with either transmitter and therefore no protocol-level information with which to distinguish them. The relevant question is whether the client can establish that the signal it is observing originates from the legitimate access point before associating with it. This requires evidence that is available to an unassociated receiver and is carried by the physical transmission itself.

FLE provides the physical-layer channel for such evidence, but any information embedded in an unprotected FLE stream can also be reproduced by a rogue transmitter. Authentication therefore requires a secret that determines the FLE signal but is unavailable to the rogue transmitter. Section 5.4 introduces the second application, SpectralSeal, in which the legitimate access point uses FLE to embed a time-varying cryptographic commitment into its carrier frequency. A receiver with knowledge of the corresponding public anchor can verify the commitment directly from the received signal, while a rogue access point that lacks the secret cannot generate the same sequence. The section evaluates this approach against several implemented rogue access points.

5.2 UnderTone

With the targets stated, we now build the first application that serves them. UnderTone turns FLE into a complete general-purpose link on the ESP32 microcontroller, supplying the framing, the modulation and coding scheme, the rate selection, and the receive chain that the raw carrier-offset channel of Chapter 4 does not provide on its own. Although the techniques used to place FLE on COTS hardware are specific to the ESP32-C5, the higher-layer abstractions explained in this chapter remain agnostic to the specific firmware mechanisms used to induce and obtain CFO measurements. Consequently, any microcontroller with suitable APIs, whether exposed or reverse-engineered, could support UnderTone. A wide range of potential devices exists [43], and further research will expand the family of devices capable of supporting UnderTone.

5.2.1 Modulation and Coding Scheme

The performance of UnderTone depends on both the characteristics of the underlying Wi-Fi traffic and the quality of signal reception. As described in Section 4.2.3, we identify two primary classes of channel impairments: noise, which limits the ability to distinguish between adjacent tones, and carrier availability, which determines whether the underlying device is transmitting Wi-Fi packets from which CFO measurements can be obtained. To accommodate these impairments, UnderTone defines a configurable modulation and coding scheme (MCS) that allows the transmitter to trade data rate for robustness. Each MCS is defined by three parameters: the modulation order M~\tilde{M}, the symbol rate multiplier rr, and the amount of Reed–Solomon forward error correction (FEC).

The modulation order determines the number of distinct frequency tones used to represent each symbol. UnderTone supports four modulation orders, M~∈{2,4,8,16}\tilde{M} \in \{2,4,8,16\}. Each symbol therefore carries log2M~\log_2\tilde{M} bits. Increasing M~\tilde{M} increases the data rate by encoding more bits per symbol, but reduces the frequency separation between adjacent tones. Because UnderTone relies on CFO measurements from the underlying Wi-Fi receiver, reduced tone spacing decreases the tolerance to CFO-estimation noise and increases the likelihood of adjacent-tone misclassification. Thus, M~\tilde{M} provides a trade-off between throughput and robustness to noise.

The symbol rate is controlled independently by the rate multiplier r∈{1,2,4,8}r \in \{1,2,4,8\}. The symbol duration is defined relative to a base symbol duration of 200 ms as

T~s=200msr.\tilde{T}_s = \frac{200~\text{ms}}{r}.(5.1)

Increasing rr therefore increases the symbol rate by shortening the symbol duration. However, shorter symbols provide fewer underlying Wi-Fi packets from which to obtain and average CFO measurements. Consequently, rr provides a second trade-off between data rate and the reliability and availability of CFO measurements.

The four modulation orders and four rate multipliers form 16 modulation configurations. The M~\tilde{M}-ary tone constellation is symmetric about the carrier baseline and spans a total frequency swing of fd=30,000f_d = 30{,}000 Hz. The frequency offset assigned to tone index k~\tilde{k} is

fd,k~=−fd2+a~k~fdM~−1.f_{d,\tilde{k}}=-\frac{f_d}{2}+\tilde{a}_{\tilde{k}}\frac{f_d}{\tilde{M}-1}.(5.2)

The resulting inter-tone spacing is

Δtone=fdM~−1.\Delta_{\text{tone}} = \frac{f_d}{\tilde{M}-1}.(5.3)

Symbol-to-tone mapping uses Gray coding so that an adjacent-tone misclassification produces the minimum possible number of bit errors. The 16 modulation configurations are summarized in Table 5.1.

Each modulation configuration can be paired with one of four FEC profiles, resulting in 64 total MCS configurations. FEC is designed to mitigate both classes of channel impairments. Channel-availability impairments are given priority in decoding, however, as they are found to be more common in a typical Wi-Fi link.

The FEC profile specifies the number of Reed–Solomon parity bytes assigned to each codeword row. Because each row of the interleaved matrix forms an independent RS codeword, the required parity per row remains small even when the aggregate parity transmitted over the air is substantial. The available FEC profiles and their corresponding correction capabilities are given in Table 5.2.
